hashing-python-functions::0.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::0.snippetHtml:
For the past two years, I've developed my machine learning projects with JAX and Equinox. The basis of JAX's power is how flexibly we can compose our computation graphs by writing in a functional paradigm, using transformations like grad, vmap, and jit. But the substance of its power is PyTrees, or the ability to transform over different types of tree-structured inputs in a unified way.

To be clear: "a PyTree" is code for "some nested composition of nodes, which JAX knows how to treat like any other tree because it's been told how to flatten and unflatten the nodes". Technically every Python object is a PyTree, even if it can only be treated as just a single, unstructured leaf.

hashing-python-functions::9.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::9.snippetHtml:
Similarly, we can use selectors to specify partial initializations of model states. When working with JAX, we typically compose models as trees of Equinox Module objects. Each module node may have leaves which are its parameters; it may also be callable, and specify a transformation of the model state. But to keep the model purely functional, state cannot live inside the modules themselves: it must be passed around separately.

This is the approach I used when designing Feedbax.

hashing-python-functions::10.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::10.snippetHtml: Note: as of March 2026, I no longer use hierarchical state objects/passing, but instead use a dict-like state object, similar to what Equinox uses for stateful operations.

hashing-python-functions::12.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::12.snippetHtml: States typically have default initializations, but users may want to provide custom initializations for some part(s) of the state, without needing to construct the entire PyTree themselves. We might provide the custom initializations as a mapping from selectors, which specify the part(s) of the state to initialize, to the respective data to initialize with.

hashing-python-functions::13.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::13.snippetHtml: Suppose we are given a PyTree of default model states (i.e. arrays), and we'd like to initialize some of its leaves using custom arrays. For each leaf we want to initialize, we could pair its selector with appropriate leaf values to assign to the selected subtree. But maybe we don't know beforehand exactly which leaves we'll want to initialize, so we'd like a general tool that can perform the initialization for us in any case:

def replace_nodes(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[tuple[Callable, Any]]):

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree

def replace_nodes(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[tuple[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, node_value in spec:
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, node_value)
    return tree
```

hashing-python-functions::15.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::15.snippetHtml: This works, so long as the structure of the node values matches the structure of their respective selector's return value. However, of course some of our selectors might pick out trees containing redundant leaves from tree, and in that case we'll end up pointlessly replacing the same leaf more than once. Perhaps it is better to assume in this case that our selectors will specify individual, unique leaves (or at least, trees of non-intersecting subsets of leaves). So, suppose instead we use the function:

hashing-python-functions::16.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::16.snippetHtml:
def replace_leaves(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[dict[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, leaf_value in spec.items():
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, leaf_value)
    return tree

some_other_init_data: Array

hashing-python-functions::26.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::26.snippetHtml: What is responsible for this weirdness? Well, Python accesses and assigns dict entries based on the uniqueness of a key's hash... and this doesn't work like you might think, or like I once naively hoped, when the key happens to be a function.

hashing-python-functions::27.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::28.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::28.snippetHtml: Any Python object that can be hashed[^2] can be used as a key in a dict. While a Python function is hashable, its hash is based on its object identity, which in CPython (i.e. for almost all Python users) is just its memory address. For example, all of the following expressions evaluate to False:

hashing-python-functions::29.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::29.snippetHtml:
# Explicitly compare by object identity
id(lambda x: x) == id(lambda x: x)
(lambda x: x) is (lambda x: x)

# Implicitly compare by object identity
(lambda x: x) == (lambda x: x)
...
hashing-python-functions::29.codeText:
```python
# Explicitly compare by object identity
id(lambda x: x) == id(lambda x: x)
(lambda x: x) is (lambda x: x)

# Implicitly compare by object identity
(lambda x: x) == (lambda x: x)

# Explicitly compare by hash
hash(lambda x: x) == hash(lambda x: x)
```

hashing-python-functions::30.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::30.snippetHtml: Since these will evaluate False for any function, and since selectors are of course "any function", this example is also False:

hashing-python-functions::31.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::31.codeText:
```python
hash(lambda model: model.some_layer) == hash(lambda model: model.some_layer)
```

hashing-python-functions::32.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::32.snippetHtml: At first this might seem kind of weird. Not only is lambda model: model.some_layer obviously identical to lambda model: model.some_layer in how it's written (i.e. its structure, or syntax), but the two are also obviously identical in how we should expect them to behave (i.e. their meaning, or semantics). Actually, in the case of a subtree selector, syntax and semantics are pretty closely aligned in general: once we know its syntax then we can be pretty certain about what it is going to return, and vice versa, since it's just performing some simple accesses of parts of a data structure.

hashing-python-functions::33.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::33.snippetHtml: If functions were hashed in those terms, then our selectors' uniqueness would be determined just like we want it to be. Seems pretty useful! So why wouldn't Python evaluate hashes or equivalence, in terms of either syntax or semantics?

hashing-python-functions::34.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::34.snippetHtml: Semantics? That's easy. And by "easy", of course I mean impossible: it's a well-known mathematical fact that there's no general method by which we can test whether any two functions will always behave the same way, for all inputs. So if programming language designers want tools like hash and == operators to be general-purpose, and useful for comparing any two functions their users might write, then those tools can't be based on semantic comparisons which are necessarily not general.

hashing-python-functions::35.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::35.snippetHtml: We could also try to evaluate equivalence in terms of syntax, which is the structure of the function's code. This is at least possible, when we have access to the code. But for arbitrary functions it can get expensive: parsing source, building ASTs, and normalizing for trivial differences such as variable names. Perhaps it's enough most of the time to know that two functions aren't literally identical in memory, which is what we test with a direct hash comparison.

hashing-python-functions::36.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::36.snippetHtml: Since dict uses hash to determine the uniqueness of keys, and the hash of a selector is not determined by what it picks out, dict cannot see our selectors the way we see them...

hashing-python-functions::38.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::38.snippetHtml: Once upon a time I decided that I really wanted to be able to use subtree selectors as dict keys. But I knew selectors don't hash in terms of the part(s) of a PyTree they access. So I decided to make a custom type of dict that did not directly (mis)treat them as keys, but instead converted them to an intermediate value which would hash on my terms. For that, I needed a function that takes a selector as input, and returns a hashable representation of its syntax as output.

It's pretty cheap, since we just need to compare the strings character-by-character until there is a single mismatch. However, it's pretty naive, and hardly useful. Consider that none of the following functions will test as equivalent if we compare them literally, though their differences are trivial:

hashing-python-functions::52.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::52.snippetHtml: An Abstract syntax tree (AST) is a data structure specifically intended to represent the syntax of a program. Python's ast implementation would say that all of the functions in the previous example have equivalent ASTs. However it, like most AST implementations, includes the naming of bound variables as part of the syntax. So for example:

hashing-python-functions::53.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::53.snippetHtml:
def compare_ast(*code: str):
    tree_dumps = [ast.dump(ast.parse(s)) for s in code]
    return len(set(tree_dumps)) == 1

compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda x: (x)")  # True
compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda y: y")  # False; the only difference is a bound variable name
...
hashing-python-functions::53.codeText:
```python
def compare_ast(*code: str):
    tree_dumps = [ast.dump(ast.parse(s)) for s in code]
    return len(set(tree_dumps)) == 1

compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda x: (x)")  # True
compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda y: y")  # False; the only difference is a bound variable name
```

hashing-python-functions::54.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::54.snippetHtml: There are good reasons why we'd want to preserve bound variable names in ASTs, but when testing for the syntactic equivalence of functions, we generally admit alpha equivalence. Normalizing our ASTs to an alpha-equivalent form can require a little work when dealing with arbitrarily complex functions with nested scopes of bound variables.

hashing-python-functions::55.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::55.snippetHtml: When a programming language designer implements an operator like == for arbitrary comparisons, they don't know how complex the objects to be compared will be. If they base the comparison on structure, then in certain cases a very large amount of work may be implied. Instead, it makes sense to base comparisons on unique ID (e.g. memory address) so that we can tell whether two references are to the same object, while leaving more complex structural comparisons to be implemented by developers on top of the language base.

hashing-python-functions::56.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::57.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::57.snippetHtml: Once Python has parsed the literal source code, it encodes the program as a sequence of lower-level instructions for the interpreter to run. Therefore, bytecode is language-dependent; bytecode in Python looks different than bytecode for a different interpreted language. Parsing does involve some semantic interpretation, and unlike an AST, bytecode is not mainly intended as a representation of syntax. But we can imagine the syntax of the resulting bytecode as a practical substitute for our source syntax.

hashing-python-functions::58.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::58.snippetHtml: So in some cases, it might make sense to compare the bytecode of two functions, to test for some kind of equivalence.

import dis


def get_where_str(where_func: Callable) -> str:

hashing-python-functions::59.codeText:
```python
from collections.abc import Callable
import dis


def get_where_str(where_func: Callable) -> str:
    """
    Returns a string representation of the (nested) attributes accessed by a function.

    Only works for functions that take a single argument, and return that argument,
    or a single (nested) attribute accessed from the argument.
    """
    bytecode = dis.Bytecode(where_func)
    return ".".join(
        instr.argrepr for instr in bytecode
        if instr.opname == "LOAD_ATTR"
    )
```

hashing-python-functions::60.snippetHtml: But this is inflexible. It only works for a single attribute access chain. To make it work for arbitrarily complex subtrees would require more elaborate bytecode parsing.

Another common use case for a subtree selector is to define the parts of a model which will be trained:

hashing-python-functions::75.snippetHtml: It can be costly to encode functions as data (e.g. an AST). But since we're working with selectors in particular, we can just use where_func_to_str to convert them to an equivalent representation which is easily serialisable:

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from operator import attrgetter

from jaxtyping import PyTree


def attr_str_tree_to_where_func(tree: PyTree[str, 'T']) -> Callable[[PyTree], PyTree[Any, 'T']]:
    """Reverse transformation to `where_func_to_attr_str_tree`.

    Takes a PyTree of strings describing attribute accesses, and returns a function
    that returns a PyTree of attributes.

    Note: This handles attribute accesses only. Extending to handle item accesses
    (e.g. dict keys, list indices) would require parsing the bracket notation
    from the string representation.
    """
    getters = jt.map(lambda s: attrgetter(s), tree)

    def where_func(obj):
        return jt.map(lambda g: g(obj), getters)

    return where_func
```

hashing-python-functions::79.title: Hashing functions by what they select

hashing-python-functions::81.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::81.snippetHtml: While Python can't hash arbitrary functions by their behaviour (impossible) or their syntax (expensive), subtree selectors are constrained enough that we can trace their execution with a custom object and regenerate exactly which paths they access. This lets us construct a hashable representation that matches our intuition about when two selectors are "the same."

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar

import equinox as eqx
import jax.tree as jt
from jax.tree_util import register_pytree_node_class
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree


T = TypeVar('T')


def _where_to_str(where: Callable) -> str:
    """Return a single string representing an accessor function."""
    terms = where_func_to_attr_str_tree(where)
    if isinstance(terms, str):
        where_str = terms
    else:
        where_str = ", ".join(jt.leaves(terms))
    return where_str

@register_pytree_node_class
class WhereDict(AbstractTransformedOrderedDict[str, Callable[[PyTree], Any], T]):
    """An `OrderedDict` that allows use of accessor functions as keys.

    In particular, keys can be callables (functions/lambdas) that take a single argument,
    and return a PyTree of leaves, as visited by attribute/item accesses.

    Functions are parsed to strings, which can be used interchangeably as keys.
    For example, the following return the same value when `init_spec` is a `WhereDict`:

    > init_spec[lambda state: state.mechanics.effector]
    > init_spec['mechanics.effector']

    Finally, a `tuple[Callable, str]` may also be provided as a key, for cases where
    different unique entries must be included for the same callable. For example,
    the following are equivalent:

    > init_spec[(lambda state: state.mechanics.effector, "first")]
    > init_spec['mechanics.effector#first']

    Note that the hash symbol `#` is used as a delimiter in the string representation.

    ??? Note "Performance"
        For typical initialization mappings (1-10 items) construction is on the order
        of 50x slower than `OrderedDict`. Access is about 2-20x slower, depending
        whether indexed by string or by callable.

        However, we only need to do a single construction and a single access of
        init_spec per batch/evaluation, so performance shouldn't matter too much in
        practice: the added overhead is <50 us/batch, and a batch normally takes
        at least 20,000 us to train.
    """

    def _key_transform(self, key: str | Callable | tuple[Callable, str]) -> str:
        return self.key_transform(key)

    @staticmethod
    def key_transform(key: str | Callable | tuple[Callable, str]) -> str:

        if isinstance(key, str):
            pass
        elif isinstance(key, Callable):
            where_str = _where_to_str(key)
            return where_str
        elif isinstance(key, tuple):
            if not isinstance(key[0], Callable) or not isinstance(key[1], str):
                raise ValueError("Each `WhereDict` key should be supplied as a string, "
                                 "a callable, or a tuple of a callable and a string")
            where_str = _where_to_str(key[0])
            return '#'.join([where_str, key[1]])
        else:
            raise ValueError("Each `WhereDict` key should be supplied as a string, "
                             "a callable, or a tuple of a callable and a string")
        return key

    def __repr__(self):
        return eqx.tree_pformat(self)
```

hashing-python-functions::88.title: Hashing functions by what they select
hashing-python-functions::88.snippetHtml: [^1]: Sometimes I call these where-functions for short, since “selector” might be misinterpreted: note that a subtree selector returns a tree, not a structureless container. However, I also use “selector” when I think it is clear. [^2]: That is, any object the builtin function hash can take as an input, returning a unique string.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::0.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::0.snippetHtml: Can you imagine what kind of personality you’d have if you could run away almost magically, as soon as you felt like it, no matter the situation?

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::1.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::1.snippetHtml: You’ve just imagined what it’s like to be a bird.[^1] No sense of propriety, decorum, proportion. Don’t like something? Date going poorly, perhaps? Take to the heavens! Find somewhere new! Erratic little shits.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::2.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::2.snippetHtml: What an apt slur. For oh, how they shit.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::3.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::3.snippetHtml: The white stuff is uric acid. That’s how they get rid of extra nitrogen: as an opaque solid.[^2] Apparently, some people appreciate these donations. To me, they seem gratuitous at best. The Earth already has lots of nitrogen for the taking. The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen!

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::4.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::4.snippetHtml: Despite a bird’s relative lack of chill, it does enjoy atmosphere. But though its poop’s paleness is nitrogenous, it isn’t the proceeds of the tropospheric air, not proximally. It’s the product of protein, processing inward through the cursed gut of the thing, entering via the clickety little beak on its freaky little face.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::5.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::5.snippetHtml: You (yes, you) also have extra nitrogen to get rid of. Haven’t you noticed? You discard it as urea though, not as uric acid. Urea likes to be wet, so it isn’t white when you leak it out.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::6.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::6.snippetHtml: Some skin creams contain urea. And because urea likes to be wet, it pulls water into your skin. Your hands get softer.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::7.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::7.snippetHtml: I guess it might go without saying, but you shouldn’t urinate on yourself as an alternative to conventional skincare.[^3]

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::8.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::8.snippetHtml: The martlet is a bird without feet. It isn’t real, though. A mythical ornithical. According to Wikipedia, it “never roosts from the moment of its drop-birth until its death fall; martlets are proposed to be constantly on the wing. This condition is an allegory for continuous effort”.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::10.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::10.snippetHtml: A martlet is a sort of beacon of virtue. I especially respect that it never insinuates its unorthodox body into terrestrial affairs.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::11.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::11.snippetHtml: Can you tell that I’m trying to find my authorial voice? Leeleeleeleelee!

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::12.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::12.snippetHtml: Unfortunately, I’ll never tweet as well as a bird. My ancestors grew a larynx, which is basically a flute made of a couple of muscle-tensioned sheets of meat. Revolutionary, at the time. A bird, on the other hand, has a syrinx. This means it has two flutes instead of one, with meat that jiggles even faster than ours can.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::13.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::13.snippetHtml: I’m not envious; the Earth already has lots of meat for the taking. Now, if only I weren’t terminally confused about whether I should be a vegan...

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::14.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::14.snippetHtml: Birds have better lungs than us. Is there no end to the humiliation?[^4]

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::15.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::15.snippetHtml: Our lungs are made of many little bags that fill and unfill with air. The air in the middle of the bag isn’t absorbed very well on account of being in buttfuck nowhere, alveolarly speaking.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::16.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::16.snippetHtml: Birds, in an act of utterly-smugly-insufferable evolution, developed the following solution: they pull the air into bags (bigger than ours…) that elegantly absorb nothing. Then they push it out of the bags and through a series of tubes. Blood vessels run across the tubes. Something-something physics, something-something higher ceiling on the amount of oxygen absorbed.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::17.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::17.snippetHtml: This setup is really helpful to birds because of how much time they spend in flight, away from everything and everyone, at unconscionably hypoxic altitudes.[^5]

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::18.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::18.snippetHtml: For a similar reason, birds also have stronger hearts than us.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::19.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::19.snippetHtml: Ugh. It’s enough to turn you into a conflict theorist.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::22.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::22.snippetHtml: [^2]: Uric acid doesn’t dissolve well in water, but that’s to be expected. Wells usually don’t dissolve in water, or they wouldn’t be very good wells. Good wells? I repeat myself.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::23.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::23.snippetHtml: [^3]: Unless your urine happens to be hand lotion. Who am I to judge?

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::24.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::24.snippetHtml: [^4]: It almost makes me feel okay about the massive human experiments into chicken concentration camps.

series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::25.title: Bird, bird, bird (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-bird-bird-bird::25.snippetHtml: [^5]: It also has the unsettling implication that a bird, if it had voluntary control over its breathing muscles, might be able to take in a breath well before it decides to push it through the tubes and extract oxygen from it.

series-inkhaven-eggs::2.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::2.snippetHtml: It isn’t just any egg. It’s sitting in the caldera of a volcano. Maybe it represents the precarity of life?

series-inkhaven-eggs::3.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::3.snippetHtml: It took me several hours to coax StableDiffusion 1.5 (SD1.5) to lay this particular egg in January 2023. It totally failed at simple attempts like “egg sitting in the caldera of a volcano”, so instead I started by using the AND keyword to produce the intersection of two prompts:[^1]

series-inkhaven-eggs::8.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::8.snippetHtml: But a simple AND of these prompts wasn’t enough to get the result I wanted. Instead, I’d invariably be given some magmatic variant of your boring old egg-in-a-cup.

series-inkhaven-eggs::10.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::10.snippetHtml: I suppose this was because the joint egg+cup was much stronger than in SD1.5’s training set than egg+caldera.

series-inkhaven-eggs::11.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::11.snippetHtml: To sneak past that, I weighted the egg-in-a-cup prompt more highly for the first 2-4 denoising steps, then quickly turned up the weight on egg-in-a-caldera. The idea was to get the model to put the egg into a noisy proto-cup, thereby locking in the correct overall cup-like composition, but then while the cup’s form was still ambiguous, turn up egg-in-a-caldera.

series-inkhaven-eggs::12.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::12.snippetHtml: Here are are two results from during that tuning process. The one on the left is fully egg-in-cup. The one on the right is somewhere in between, the weights being switched too late, and the cup too well established already to be diffused into a volcano.

series-inkhaven-eggs::14.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::14.snippetHtml: Here are a few other eggs-in-caldera that I generated with SD1.5 from different seeds.

series-inkhaven-eggs::18.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::18.snippetHtml: Eggs and egg-shaped portals have become my preferred objects to prompt for, when evaluating the aesthetics of image models. In the process I think I’ve become something of an eggspert on what makes a good egg, as well as what to eggspect from each model.

series-inkhaven-eggs::19.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::19.snippetHtml: In the neggst section I’ll show results from some other models. None of them allow advanced parametrization like AND, or weight adjustments over denoising steps, or most of the other fancy things we can do when working with local models like StableDiffusion. But why not?

series-inkhaven-eggs::20.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::20.snippetHtml: For one, the frontier labs haven’t been much for giving that level of parametric control over their cloud models in any case. And as models have gotten better at thinking and composition, the eggspectation is that you should be able to simply describe what you want prosaically, and the model will figure everything out for you.

series-inkhaven-eggs::21.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::21.snippetHtml: While compositionality and prompt understanding have both improved, I agree with others that the results have lately become less iconic or weird, and more like quality, all-purpose trough fodder. But the purpose of this post not to talk about model collapse or regression to the mean or whatever you think is the cause of ensloppification. This post is eggs.

series-inkhaven-eggs::22.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::22.snippetHtml: If this were a rigorous eggsperiment, I would have done some things differently, such as giving a standard set of prompts to each model in turn, for a fairer set of comparisons. But this was not rigorous. This was eggs.

series-inkhaven-eggs::26.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::26.snippetHtml: Eggsample prompt (bottom left): cosmic egg, pristine yolk, divine whites, smooth shell, sunburst, bicolor, woodcut bliss --no frame

series-inkhaven-eggs::29.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::29.snippetHtml: Eggsample prompt (right): psychedelic portal, smooth and pristine egg in its natural habitat --no cracked, border, rough

series-inkhaven-eggs::32.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::32.snippetHtml: Eggsample prompt (top right): doodle linotype, psychedelic portal, smooth and pristine egg in its natural habitat --no cracked, border, rough

series-inkhaven-eggs::35.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::35.snippetHtml: Eggsample prompt (top left): masterful precise illustration, unnaturally smooth egg, mystical experience involving a bird’s unhatched progeny --no smudge --weird 100

series-inkhaven-eggs::38.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::38.snippetHtml: Prompt: psychedelic color intaglio, salvador dali, smooth and pristine egg in its natural habitat --no cracked, border, rough shell, reflective

series-inkhaven-eggs::39.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::39.snippetHtml: Midjourney v6 generated decently interesting images with little prompting effort, so my strategy was a bit different than with SD1.5: generate a bunch of images and choose my favourites. This felt less like “making art” than caldera-egg did.

series-inkhaven-eggs::40.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::40.snippetHtml: I was pleased with the variability in its responses, but likewise, it had some issues with the consistency of details. For eggsample:

series-inkhaven-eggs::42.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::42.snippetHtml: Prompt: masterful precise illustration, unnaturally smooth psychedelic egg, mystical experience involving a bird’s unhatched progeny --no sane

series-inkhaven-eggs::43.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::43.snippetHtml: Kind of a mess, though reasonably symmetric compared to what SD1.5 would have done with something this intricate.

series-inkhaven-eggs::46.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::46.snippetHtml: Eggsample prompt (top left): minimalist egg containing a psychedelic portal, resting snugly in the caldera of a single volcano as if it were an egg cup, in a psychedelic ukiyo-e landscape

series-inkhaven-eggs::47.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::47.snippetHtml: Still low prompt effort, and the results were getting smoother and still more coherent in the details. I remember being frustrated that I was limited to prosaic prompts, but couldn’t coax it to rest the egg inside the caldera.

series-inkhaven-eggs::50.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::50.snippetHtml: Prompt: in the Orion Nebula, a brilliant egg shaped portal, through which is visible a barren stratovolcano under a clear blue sky, with a white egg sitting half-inside its caldera, as though in a cup

series-inkhaven-eggs::51.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::51.snippetHtml: This is the first time I was able to get a model to one-shot this composition, though I think the result is still less iconic than the SD1.5 caldera egg.

series-inkhaven-eggs::52.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::52.snippetHtml: And of course it still makes mistakes, such as its attempt at the netivot in this kabbalistic tree of egg:

series-inkhaven-eggs::54.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::54.snippetHtml: Prompt: in the Orion Nebula, a brilliant egg shaped portal, through which is visible a kabbalistic tree of life against a clear blue sky, where each of the 10 sefirot (11 nodes) is a pristine egg

series-inkhaven-eggs::55.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::55.snippetHtml: But the best GPT-Image-1 egg is probably this one:

series-inkhaven-eggs::57.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::57.snippetHtml: Prompt: A photo of a luminescent egg-shaped portal, through the sheen of which is imminently visible a vibrant fractal dimension; the portal is floating low above a dark, calm, and florid ukiyo-e landscape

series-inkhaven-eggs::60.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::60.snippetHtml: Prompt: a print of an egg resting in the caldera of a stratovolcano, as though it were an egg cup

series-inkhaven-eggs::62.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::62.snippetHtml: I still prefer the original caldera egg. I had to be thoughtful to create it, and it’s iconically simple. So I decided to make it my avatar recently.

series-inkhaven-eggs::63.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::63.snippetHtml: I haven’t tried the newest local models (such as Flux) to see how they compare to SD1.5. If I get a chance, I’ll mess with one for a couple of hours before I post some BONUS EGGS that did not make it into this post. Coming to a day near soon!

series-inkhaven-eggs::67.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::67.snippetHtml: (GPT-Image-1) Prompt: generate an image of an egg person in a serious egg play and they are become kind of eggy because they have forgotten one of their eggs (the image does not contain multiple actual eggs)

series-inkhaven-eggs::68.title: Eggs (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-eggs::68.snippetHtml: [^1]: I don’t have the original SD1.5 prompts with me here at Inkhaven, but I am confident in my eggsplanation of the broad strokes of my prompting strategy.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::4.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::4.snippetHtml: Maybe you never got to feel it, at all.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::6.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::6.snippetHtml: The world breaks, but love is stubborn. The hands clutch the jagged unfixable shards, the scarred unfeeling remnants, and bleed.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::7.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::7.snippetHtml: The eyes drink in the blood, and weep.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::8.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::8.snippetHtml: The hands, still holding the shards, grow stiller.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::13.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::13.snippetHtml: a hungry hoard that takes and swells and takes and swells and

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::14.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::14.snippetHtml: a mind that expands everywhere, encompasses everything, becomes everyone, and

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::19.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::19.snippetHtml: The fear of death drives us out of ignorance, and into the arms of death disguised.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::20.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::20.snippetHtml: Maybe our bodies don’t need to die.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::21.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::21.snippetHtml: Maybe they will become better later. (I hope they will become better, later.)

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::22.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::22.snippetHtml: Maybe we could keep only what most needs keeping.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::23.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::23.snippetHtml: I’m reminded of the dearness of forgetting.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::26.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::26.snippetHtml: These are my friends. These are our memories.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::27.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::27.snippetHtml: Some of them will stay. Some will fall away, into eternity.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::28.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::28.snippetHtml: Will you let them live there, or will you bleed?

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::29.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::29.snippetHtml: Think of everything you’ve never had the chance to love; of everyone you’ve never had the chance to know.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::30.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::30.snippetHtml: Think of the undiscovered places in your heart. Think of all the space you could make there.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::35.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::35.snippetHtml: Inkhaven ends today. It’s been the most meaningful month of my life.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::36.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::36.snippetHtml: Some of us came here wanting the space to write great things. We all had to confront our standards. I know the danger of standards; my own past is a vortex of perfectionism. So my main goal was not greatness (appealing as that is) but the beginnings of balance – in effort, intention, and openness. I feel a deep sense of okayness with how that turned out.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::37.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::37.snippetHtml: This is the first event where I’ve been really comfortable with myself, from the beginning. That’s partly down to the great friends in Montréal who’ve helped me to finally grow up, these past three years, and who will be there for me when I return. It’s partly because at last I have the clarity to avoid caffeine and alcohol.[^1] But partly, it’s due to some secret third thing, which has given me strength because I have not insisted on trying to name it as I interacted with the wonderful people here.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::38.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::38.snippetHtml: I do not find it easy to finish this. I keep looking at the wordcount... I already know how I feel. I trust my new friends to know. So who is this for?

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::39.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::39.snippetHtml: If you find it meaningful, then it is for you.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::40.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::40.snippetHtml: Friends, I’ve already prepared a space in my heart for you.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::41.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::41.snippetHtml: If it ever seems otherwise, you should know: it’s only because I’m still a child – and sometimes, I am afraid.

series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::42.title: In paradisum (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-in-paradisum::42.snippetHtml: [^1]: I haven't drank in months, and while I began Inkhaven at one cup of tea per day, I'm now down to zero.

series-inkhaven-lightly::0.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::0.snippetHtml: The weather’s been perfect here at Lighthaven. It was raining on my arrival and continued for about twenty-four hours, through the day of April 1, but now that seems like entirely intentional foreplay.

series-inkhaven-lightly::1.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::1.snippetHtml: Sometimes it’s almost tempting to stare directly into the sun, as if to ask for even more. But I won’t do that. I know what happens.

series-inkhaven-lightly::2.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::2.snippetHtml: It can be cold at night. During the talent show I wore three layers. I even drank a small cup of beet juice (for the nitrates) but my frigid limbs wouldn’t have it, and continued to jitter and worm their way inward.

series-inkhaven-lightly::3.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::3.snippetHtml: I don’t mean to complain. It was sub-zero and snowing only 3 days before my departure from Montréal.

series-inkhaven-lightly::4.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::4.snippetHtml: One evening I struggled to operate one of the gas fire pits. I’m not sure I ever got the gas to even flow. I checked the lines; I tried every position. Nothing. Apparently there’d been a small earthquake on the 2nd which might have tickled it into dysfunction. (I was asleep at the time, and missed out on my share of the fun.)

series-inkhaven-lightly::5.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::5.snippetHtml: I didn’t bring it up with the officials. I moved on. It’s not like the flames would’ve been more captivating on that altar, than on any of the others.

series-inkhaven-lightly::6.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::6.snippetHtml: I sleep a bit better when it’s cold. Have you noticed the same? It’s a Known Thing, as far as I recall. But memory’s slippery. And I’m not going to ask Claude for confirmation. It lives in the mines and I don’t want to go down there today.

series-inkhaven-lightly::7.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::7.snippetHtml: Yesterday I wrote an almost three-thousand-word technical post in about seven hours. That was a surprise. I’m certain I’ve written just as many words in just as short a time before, but this felt cleaner and more consequential somehow. I think my thoughts have been clearing.

series-inkhaven-lightly::8.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::8.snippetHtml: I wrote that post in the Glass Room. It’s a bright room; it lets god in through its panes. After having hiked the Stonewall-Panoramic Trail this afternoon, I’m not sure I was as reverent as I could have been, yesterday, my first time writing there.

series-inkhaven-lightly::9.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::9.snippetHtml: I went back there today after returning from the hike, but it was too warm. I felt so close to heaven, I almost started to nap. I had to leave, then I drank a small cup of tea out of ‘necessity’. It was only after the tea started working that I realized the problem had been the heat.

series-inkhaven-lightly::11.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::11.snippetHtml: I keep referring to myself as autistic in conversations. I should stop doing that.

series-inkhaven-lightly::12.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::12.snippetHtml: It’s a hand-wave, something I’ve said when I’ve felt I’ve lacked the time to talk more deeply about myself. But go ahead and ask me. I’ll show you what I am.

series-inkhaven-lightly::13.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::13.snippetHtml: “Autism” is a sickness word, isn’t it? Now, before you or anyone else leaps up to smooth that over with platitudes, I want you to see how mostly okay I am. (And what exactly would smoothness serve, if I weren’t already okay? A transient okayness, couched in a larger suffering? At best it would give me some slack.)

series-inkhaven-lightly::14.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::14.snippetHtml: I don’t need to see myself as autistic, and I don’t need to see myself as not autistic. It just isn’t that helpful. I guess I’m something more specific.

series-inkhaven-lightly::15.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::15.snippetHtml: I’ve started some focaccia dough. It’s rising in the kitchen. I’ve stretched it twice already. I might move it to the glass room in a moment. There’s a poetry reading in two hours and I want it to be ready by then.

series-inkhaven-lightly::16.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::16.snippetHtml: Yeast is slow to make its way to the Glass Room, at least on its own, so I help it. It has no trouble with reverence, once it’s there.

series-inkhaven-lightly::17.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::17.snippetHtml: I haven’t written about my intentions for Inkhaven yet.

series-inkhaven-lightly::18.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::18.snippetHtml: I do want to produce good and even impressive works. I want to say that this might not be one of them (it hasn’t taken much effort) but I’ve been led to believe that my prejudices about which of my words others will most enjoy, are probably wrong.

series-inkhaven-lightly::20.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::20.snippetHtml: More important than being impressive, though, I want to be healthy. I want my mind to be kind of smooth (uh oh) like a... like a dolphin in its medium? I want to speak from the edge of unspeakable wonder. I want my words to be something like the trees I passed in the hills today, growing and growing and smelling like fresh basil for some reason. I want to breach the surface of thought, just to fall back in again. I want to be filled with light and warmth.

series-inkhaven-lightly::21.title: Lightly (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-lightly::21.snippetHtml: The clouds have arrived as though to prove something, but the Glass Room will probably stay warm enough for long enough to make a difference in the rise.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Philip Glass

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: You’ve probably heard some music by Philip Glass (1937–). He’s a 20th century minimalist, though he doesn’t identify that way.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: He described himself as a composer of "music with repetitive structures"

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: He described himself as a composer of "music with repetitive structures"

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: His music is in fact very very repetitive. This is good because it gives you time to “get it” during your first listen. It’s not so good when you want music that changes quickly, like if you have no attention span or something.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: One thing I like is his opera Akhnaten, which tells the story of the pharaoh that decided that everyone should worship the sun disk instead of all the usual Egyptian gods. Here’s the opera’s intro, which has no singing but does have a badass narration at the end which is part of an English translation of the Egyptian Book of the Dead.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Here’s a scene with vocals. Something quite unusual about this scene is that Akhnaten (the first voice to enter) sings in a higher register than the other two characters, who are both women (his wife Nefertiti and his mother Queen Tye).

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: For good measure, here’s the Glass piece that has the most listens on Spotify.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Schubert

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Once upon a time I fell in love with a syphilitic Viennese guy that died 200 years ago. He wrote over 600 songs, and is one of the composers most responsible for how songwriting evolved in the 19th and 20th centuries. Being short and chubby, his friends gave him the nickname Schwammerl, or “little mushroom”.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Like Beethoven, Schubert is classed as both late Classical[^1] or early Romantic. But where Beethoven sometimes seems like he’s trying to beat the truth out of the universe, Schubert feels more natural and beauty-oriented.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Schubert popularized the impromptu, a kind of short single-movement piano piece. Here’s the best recording of the best impromptu.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Schubert wrote a ton of music, and I find a lot of it a little too simple to re-listen. But near the end of his short life, he wrote some really profound and intimate stuff. Here’s one of the best examples. The performer (Sviatoslav Richter) takes an unusually slow tempo, which creates an ethereal and meditative vibe.[^2]

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: The next piece is popular, usually known as Schubert’s Ave Maria and sung using the Latin words of the prayer. But this recording uses the original German text instead, which isn’t a literal translation of the Hail Mary but describes a young girl praying to Mary. It also uses a fortepiano, the kind of piano that Schubert played, which is the precursor to the modern piano.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Here’s one more piece of Schubert’s played on a fortepiano, and then a second recording by the same performer but on a modern piano:[^3]

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Chopin

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: He arrived on the scene shortly after Schubert died, and is his natural successor in a way, but more complex, technical, and Polish-flavoured instead of Viennese.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Almost everything he wrote is magical. He’s more popular than Schubert, so for now I’ll just share one of my favourite nocturnes.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Godowsky

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Leopold Godowsky was one of the best pianists of all time, and one of the musicians who added the most to the art of composing for the piano. He was also a big fan of Schubert and wrote a tribute to him: a passacaglia, which is a bunch of variations with a shared bassline. Here, the bassline comes from the beginning of Schubert’s “Unfinished” Symphony 8. Turn up the volume and listen to the first 12 seconds of this:

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Now the variations. In some of them, Godowsky ropes in other Schubert themes as well, including the famous Erlkönig.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: He also wrote a bunch of variations on Chopin’s Études. The Études are famously difficult, but Godowsky’s variations are considered some of the most difficult piano pieces ever written. For example, first consider this Chopin original:

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: And now the Godowsky’s incredible variation, called “Ignis fatuus”, which is Latin for will-o’-the-wisp, or the ghostly, dancing lights seen at night by travellers in European folklore.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Fin

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: In the future, I’ll make more posts about the music I like: Bach, Wagner, Richard Strauss, Stravinsky, and others. And maybe some non-classical stuff, too.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: [^1]: What the average person calls “classical music” (and the way I use it in the rest of the post) is an umbrella for all of the music written in the West in the last ~1200 years, that doesn’t fall under other genres like folk music, pop music, jazz, and so on. To a music historian, “Classical” means music written in the period 1750–1820; the most famous Classical composer is Mozart.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: [^2]: Schubert’s tendency to modulate to distant keys also contributes to this.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: [^3]: The entire album and its partner are some of the best albums of fortepiano music.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: It’s that time again! Let’s start with the same general advice I gave in the first part:

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml:
If you’re new to classical, here’s a bit of context:

  • Treat it like going to an art gallery. Wear headphones for the best experience. When you don’t know a piece yet, put all your attention on it, get absorbed in the detail and the harmony.
  • A big difference between classical and (say) pop music is that there usually isn’t an official version of a classical piece. Every recording is a cover, in a sense.
  • Different recordings of the same piece are made by different performers with different setups. So you can have a recording that is better in terms of feeling, but really old and fuzzy because it was made with ancient or badly-placed microphones. You can also have a crystal clear recording from 2026 where the musician plays like a soulless robot. (If you like one of the pieces here, I suggest you check out some other recordings of the piece to get a better sense of this.)
  • I’ll share Spotify links when I can, but sometimes a recording is only available on YouTube.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: One more thing

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: In this post I share a bunch of vocal pieces. Listening to classical singing (e.g. opera) is different from listening to modern singing. Before the invention of microphones and speakers and recordings, a singer had to project their voice over an entire theatre. A loud orchestra might be playing at the same time. So, classical singing is exaggerated and its dynamic range is compressed upwards. A modern singer can whisper softly into a microphone when they want to be intimate; a classical singer needs to “gently yell”. This is similar to how a stage actor uses exaggerated and audience-facing body language and facial expressions, but a film actor in closeup can depend on the smallest of their expressions being visible to viewers.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: It doesn’t take much time to get used to classical singing, but before that happens, you might find it kind of loud and flat. And there are a lot of mediocre classical singers, so the point about different recordings of the same piece becomes even more relevant.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Wagner

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: This asshole was a multimodal genius. Before him, an opera was a flowery sausage-chain of dialogues and arias, bound up in a ludicrous corset. Composers usually didn’t write the story or the words (libretto) themselves, but composed their music to fit existing texts. The grandiose took precedence over the profound.[^1]

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Wagner wanted to create a comprehensive work of art, a synthesis of all available media.[^2] He used his creative judgment to write the story, words, music, and stage directions for all his later operas. He also insisted on through-composition, meaning a continuous stream of music rather than discrete arias mingled with dialogue.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: His most famous work is Der Ring des Nibelungen (i.e. “The Ring of the Nibelung” or just “The Ring”) a four-part opera cycle composed between 1848 and 1874. The story has many similarities to The Lord of the Rings, including, among others:

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: • a ring, forged through a perverse sacrifice by the villain, gives him mastery over the world; corrupts anyone else who tries to bear it; and is returned to its origin upon its destruction;[^3]

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: The piece at the beginning of this section is the opening prelude of the cycle. It depicts sunrise on the Rhine river, which is the only real-world location mentioned in the operas. The Ring’s music is woven out of many leitmotifs which represent different aspects of the fantasy world; here, at the very start, we have an uncomplicated arpeggio which represents the purity of primordial nature.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: I’ll share just one other piece from The Ring: the funeral march of the central hero, Siegfried. He is a fearless and unconquerable warrior loved by all, until he is tricked into breaking a sacred oath, and killed by the villain’s bitter son.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Some people are obsessed with Mahler. I’m not, but I do want to share the opening movement from Das Lied von der Erde (“The Song of the Earth”), a symphony which he didn’t number as such, out of superstition.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: This movement is called Das Trinklied vom Jammer der Erde (“The Drinking Song of Earth’s Sorrow”) and is a loose translation of 悲歌行 (“Song of Sorrow”) by the famous Tang dynasty poet Li Bai.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Don’t listen to his self-deprecation. He’s one of the best. In the early 1900’s he started to transition from late Romanticism to early Modernism with his operas Salome and Elektra, but then receded back into Romanticism instead of proceeding fully into atonality. Good for him.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Salome is probably my favourite opera. If you’re new to opera, this is a good one to start with. It’s only 100 minutes long and there’s a decent film recording of it. It tells the story of the ancient Judean princess who demanded the head of John the Baptist (named “Jochanaan” in the opera). The German text is an abridged but direct translation from Oscar Wilde’s only French play, which takes a lot of artistic license with the original biblical story, and portrays Salome’s motivation as infatuation.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: Here’s the very end of the opera. Salome has successfully obtained the head on a silver platter and kissed it (“why wouldn’t you kiss me?”). She notes that he has a bitter taste on his lips, wonders aloud whether it’s the taste of love (“they say that love has a bitter taste”), then shakes her head and exalts in her victory (“what does it matter? I’ve kissed you!”) before being killed by the palace guards on the orders of her superstitious stepfather Herod.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: His next opera, Elektra, is also excellent. It’s more modernist, more polytonal, and tells revenge story of the ancient princess. Elektra wants to kill her mother Clytemnestra for having murdered her father Agamemnon (for having sacrificed their daughter Iphigenia before going off to Troy). Instead, their exiled brother Orestes (Orest in German) shows up and does the deed.

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: In this clip, Elektra’s sister has an ecstatic meltdown because she had been led to believe that Orestes was dead. The sisters share a duet before Elektra dances herself to death, ending the opera:

series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.title: Listen to this Classical Music 2 (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-listen-to-this-classical.snippetHtml: [^3]: Many of the similarities are because Wagner and Tolkien relied on the same Germanic source materials: the Nibelungenlied, the Völsunga Saga, the Eddas, and the þiðreks saga. But some things – such as all these details I mentioned about the ring, apart from its mere existence in the story – are not found in the source materials, which suggests that Tolkien might have stolen them from Wagner. Tolkien would never admit to such a thing (“Both rings were round, and there the resemblance ceases”). Some of this could be due to cultural osmosis (Wagner was all-seeping in the early 20th century) or simple convergence of ideas.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: There’s a kind of meditation that feels really, really good, called the first jhana. It’s not the same as an orgasm, but it’s comparable in intensity. Your entire body buzzes, like goosebumps on steroids. Your mind is a surging flood of euphoria. It takes some practice to get there (and this post isn’t about that) but once you do, you can stay there as long as you like.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: “That sounds scary and addictive” is a reasonable first reaction.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: For sure it can be scary. Newbies often have trouble entering the ‘bliss state’ for more than a second or two because it’s so surprising and overwhelming that their reflective mind yells something must be wrong with me, how can this be happening and kicks them back out of it.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: Addiction is rare. Instead, the blissee gets excited about the newfound experience and spends time on it regularly for some weeks. Then they start to lose interest. They also become less interested in other addictive habits, like having an extra slice of cake after dinner, or using recreational drugs like alcohol for social reasons.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: This is weird. It clashes with our usual intuitions about how pleasure grabs our attention and coerces us to seek it out – the intuitions that stop many of us from taking heroin for fun on the weekends.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: The first jhana is maximally pleasurable, but minimally reinforcing. This makes sense if there is a distinction between how our brains want, versus enjoy.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: Wanting is about some thing. My nose perks up at the first hint of dinner. My eyes flicker around the room and pick out things I might want to eat, or games I might want to play, or people I might want to have sex with, or doors I might follow to other rooms, and so on.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: Liking is just an internal state. A sign that says “Like!” pops up; enjoyment occurs. Maybe the sign pops up when we get something we want; but maybe that’s not a strict rule.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: The first jhana is anti-addictive because it cultivates enjoyment that’s free of any particular desire – the internal state, unhooked from external temptation. By entering this state, we get embodied evidence that undermines the map-territory confusion which says that enjoyment lives in the external object of desire, and can’t be had without that object. Actually, the enjoyment lives in you. The object is incidental. Another object, a more healthy or virtuous object, could do just as well.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: As long as you haven’t internalized that, the objects of your desire hold a tyranny over your mind. Your current conception of what you should desire might be pretty good, but in hindsight it’ll still be inadequate. And you are at its mercy. But when you know that whatever you currently desire doesn’t hold a monopoly over your enjoyment, then you have the freedom to make better choices with less fear of personal sacrifice.

series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.title: Meditative bliss states are the opposite of reward hacking (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-meditative-bliss-states-.snippetHtml: Naively, the first jhana looks like reward hacking. But for human brains, addiction means being hooked-in to sensations from the world. The first jhana teaches us to see beyond that.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::0.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::0.snippetHtml: It's always the right time to think. So go on, think some more. You’ve probably forgotten to consider some edge cases. You should agonize a bit longer. If you don’t, someone will beat you to it. You’ll miss something. They won’t. They’re already finding the newest game to play. You don’t even know how to start looking for it. Prepare to be embarrassed and defeated.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::1.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::1.snippetHtml: You worthless piece of shit, you’re definitely gonna be part of the permanent underclass.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::2.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::2.snippetHtml: Traders are varying degrees of pretentious and paranoid. And why shouldn’t they be? They make more money than you. They expose themselves to more information than you. Obviously they’re in the right position to make all the important decisions. They’re stretching their intelligence to the limit. And all for the market, which is the world, practically speaking. We should thank them! Things are as good as they are, because of traders. They’re at the frontier of all that matters. Of course they’re better than you.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::3.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::3.snippetHtml: They don’t need to say it, though. It’s self-evident, and void of alpha.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::4.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::4.snippetHtml: You know that “red button versus blue button” thought experiment that’s been lurching around the internet like an excessively fresh corpse?

series-inkhaven-negative-space::5.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::5.snippetHtml: My friends fixated on this question for a day or two. They’ve fixated on similar questions before. Every time, the sickness is short, but they’re always ready to be infected again.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::6.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::6.snippetHtml: After all, if we don’t think through the problem, the red button pushers might get us. Death. Death. DEATH!

series-inkhaven-negative-space::7.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::7.snippetHtml: The question kept our group chat occupied. I responded, but I wasn’t eloquent. I failed to express that 1) of course I agree we should be thoughtful, and that whether people press red or blue depends on where they live, and how long they think it through, and whether they get to push the button for their children, and… … but also 2) that they were sniped so easily by the question made it clear that they had a hidden tendency to self-harm.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::8.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::8.snippetHtml: One of them, understandably misunderstanding me, implied that I was succumbing to the chaos of controversy. You angry, bro?

series-inkhaven-negative-space::9.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::9.snippetHtml: No. I’m willing to die if it means that the world will be more than 50% blue pushers, forever. I think some of my friends would claim the same,[^1] but the more they’re fixated on the button question, the less I believe them.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::10.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::10.snippetHtml: Not that my willingness to die even means anything here. How could anyone prove that my death would achieve such an outcome? I guess I’d need to be a trader to have access to that information. But then I almost certainly wouldn’t be willing to sacrifice myself. Catch-22.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::11.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::11.snippetHtml: Wisdom and intelligence are not the same thing. Do you know when not to think? Do you even know how? Do you think that you can gain an understanding of negative space by applying your frantic brushstrokes over the entire canvas? Don’t be silly. You are incompetent.

series-inkhaven-negative-space::12.title: Negative space (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-negative-space::12.snippetHtml: Go – sit down. Close your eyes, but not to sleep. Practice not thinking until you stop frantically pooping ink all over the page while secretly, in that place you paper over with rationality, you flee like a child from annihilation.
