series-inkhaven-two-poems::34.title: Two Poems (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-two-poems::34.snippetHtml: This morning, we went to Muir Woods. I love forests, and Muir Woods is a forest.

series-inkhaven-two-poems::36.title: Two Poems (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-two-poems::36.snippetHtml: I loved it there. When I got back, I went insane. For the first time since I got to Inkhaven, I went to my room, to write at the desk there, alone. It was covered in my things, and I had to move them aside. I sat there for 20 minutes trying to write a high-effort thing before I became too agitated to stay. I left and walked around the grounds. I saw people sitting around and talking, enjoying themselves. I wasn’t enjoying anything. After 15 min of this, Cate Hall’s Q&A started, so I went to listen to that, because I like her writing. I was not happy to be there.

series-inkhaven-two-poems::37.title: Two Poems (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-two-poems::37.snippetHtml: By the end I was feeling better. I knew what I actually wanted was to be in the forest, still. But writing poetry is kind of like that. I knew I wanted to write poetry.

series-inkhaven-two-poems::38.title: Two Poems (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-two-poems::38.snippetHtml: Writing 500 words of poetry is difficult, but I already had the renga finished, and conq rightly advised me to also write about my process.

series-inkhaven-two-poems::39.title: Two Poems (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-two-poems::39.snippetHtml: How did I write the sonnet? I started by vibing out the line-ending rhymes, the vertebrae of the imagery I felt I wanted. Here: screaming-dreaming, leer-fear, choice-voice, cling-sing. I also knew I wanted the imagery to be musical. Then, I thought about how to arrange the backbone, while attempting to sound out some lines in my head. This gradually transitioned into writing out the lines more systematically, top-to-bottom, though I also quickly formed and held onto a sense of the final couplet, which helped to bind together the narrative of the poem as I wrote the intervening lines. Finally I reviewed it and thought about key phrasing choices. Here, I originally had “music” and “self-abusic”, but one unorthodox word (“ensqualored”) seemed enough for this poem.

series-inkhaven-two-poems::40.title: Two Poems (Inkhaven)
series-inkhaven-two-poems::40.snippetHtml: There are several kinds of sonnet, but this is a Shakespearean sonnet, which is the kind I tend to write. It consists of three quatrains with alternating rhymes, followed by a single rhyming couplet. So, 14 lines total. The meter is of course iambic pentameter.

series-probability-theory-channels::0.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::0.snippetHtml: Sometimes, a simple function doesn't seem good enough.

series-probability-theory-channels::1.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::1.snippetHtml: Here's one possible function we can draw, going from a set of players to a set of dice rolls.

series-probability-theory-channels::3.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::3.snippetHtml: There are other, similar functions we could choose by changing where the arrows end... but any single function like this one can only give us a single outcome for each player.

series-probability-theory-channels::4.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::4.snippetHtml: As a model of dice rolling, this function is pretty useless! Each time a player rolls, hopefully there's actually a 1/6 (or about 17%) chance of each number turning up, not a 100% chance of just one of them.

series-probability-theory-channels::7.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::7.snippetHtml: Let's try writing our diagrams a little differently. Focus just on Max, for a second. He rolls five times: 5, 1, 2, 4, 2.

series-probability-theory-channels::8.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::8.snippetHtml: Let's merge all the arrows that arrive at the same place into single arrows. An arrow's thickness represents how frequently we follow it—so the arrow that arrives at 2 is thicker than the others.

series-probability-theory-channels::10.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::10.snippetHtml: We can show the same thing using a histogram.

series-probability-theory-channels::12.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::12.snippetHtml: Now divide his roll counts by 5—the number of times he rolled. This gives a normalized histogram in terms of the fraction of total rolls that turn up each way.

series-probability-theory-channels::14.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::14.snippetHtml: Now that we've normalized the counts, the sum of all the points in the histogram is 1, or 100%.

series-probability-theory-channels::16.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::16.snippetHtml: When we've got fractions that sum to one – or percentages that sum to 100% – across a set of outcomes, we have a probability distribution.

series-probability-theory-channels::17.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::17.snippetHtml: Our distribution says: given that Max is rolling the dice, there is a 100% chance that one of the six sides will turn up. According to what we've seen, 20% of the time Max arrives at 1, 40% of the time at 2, and so on.

series-probability-theory-channels::18.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::18.snippetHtml: Now split up the histogram bars, and arrange them vertically.

series-probability-theory-channels::19.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::19.snippetHtml: Of course, five rolls isn't enough to get a good model of six-sided dice! We can't even roll once for every side. But if Max keeps rolling and rolling for a while, and we draw up all his rolls, hopefully we'll end up with something more uniform.

series-probability-theory-channels::21.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::21.snippetHtml: Whichever distribution we arrive at, at least we're now in a better position to model dice rolls when the outcome isn't fixed to one value or another.

series-probability-theory-channels::22.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::22.snippetHtml: Two classic perspectives on probability are frequentism and Bayesianism.

series-probability-theory-channels::23.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::23.snippetHtml: It's rather frequentist of us to build a probability distribution for dice rolls by getting Max to roll the dice over and over while we count the results – and expect that eventually, our percentages will settle on the "true" distribution.

series-probability-theory-channels::24.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::24.snippetHtml: The Bayesian perspective is a bit more difficult to explain.

series-probability-theory-channels::25.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::25.snippetHtml: Bayesianism does not fixate on experiments that repeat as long as possible and eventually converge on the truth independently of the strength of our prior beliefs.

series-probability-theory-channels::26.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::26.snippetHtml: We always start with some knowledge. Often we have an idea of how likely an outcome of some process is, even when we've never sampled that process before.

series-probability-theory-channels::27.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::27.snippetHtml: All knowledge is connected. If we know enough about dice manufacturing and classical physics, we may be able to convincingly argue that the probability of rolling each number is about 1/6, without having rolled the dice even once. And even when we can't explicitly support our beliefs on knowledge from other areas of life, our rather huge brains provide us with intuitions that start to become useful well before we've made them explicit.

series-probability-theory-channels::28.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::28.snippetHtml: If I'm a Bayesian, I might hold a 1/6 prior belief for any reason at all. It might be hard for me to explain why I hold it, yet. But when my friend hands me dice and I roll 4 five times in a row – according to my prior belief, the chance of that is only about 0.01% – I'll have to start to update my belief to reflect that his dice are probably not fair.

series-probability-theory-channels::29.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::29.snippetHtml: From a Bayesian perspective, it isn't that repeated experiments (or significance tests) are useless – they're just one kind of tool we can use to update our beliefs. And they're limited by how they frame our questions: through a repeatable experiment with well-defined outcomes. But to be repeatable, the context in which it makes sense to perform the experiment must itself be predictable. Do we start from predictable, or do we arrive there?

series-probability-theory-channels::30.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::30.snippetHtml: Of course, we can still use frequentist tools. In practice, their limitations are manageable when we put enough effort into predicting (or maintaining) the contexts in which it makes sense to perform repeated experiments.

series-probability-theory-channels::32.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::32.snippetHtml: To properly model probability, we'll use channels. Here's an abstract example:

series-probability-theory-channels::33.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::33.snippetHtml: For each point in the source set, we get an entire distribution on the target, just like we did for Max's dice rolls.

series-probability-theory-channels::34.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::34.snippetHtml: Whenever we draw a channel, any arrows that start at the same point will have the same color – and form a distribution. There's two source points in our last example, so there's two (vertical) histograms—one blue, one orange.

series-probability-theory-channels::35.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::35.snippetHtml: The bars of different colors grouped under each point in the target don't need to form a distribution. Here's a different channel between the same source and target sets:

series-probability-theory-channels::37.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::37.snippetHtml: There's an 85% or a 95% chance that we'll arrive at $y_3$ when we start from $x_1$ or $x_2$, respectively. So the bars under $y_3$ sum to 180%, and of course that doesn't form a distribution. But all three blue bars sum to 100%, as do all three orange.

series-probability-theory-channels::38.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::38.snippetHtml: At the start of this series, I said we'd be dealing with functions. Now I've said that we'll be working with channels. But don't channels break the rules of functions? Multiple arrows start at the same place!

series-probability-theory-channels::39.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::39.snippetHtml: Well, when we want to get formal about it, a channel really can be seen as a function. It's just not as simple as the functions we've seen so far.

series-probability-theory-channels::40.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::40.snippetHtml: A "simple" function looks like $f\to Y$, where $X$ and $Y$ are sets of outcomes. This won't work for probability, since for each $x\in X$, we can only reach a single outcome $y\in Y$ with 100% probability.

series-probability-theory-channels::41.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::41.snippetHtml: Now, say we also have a fancy function $\mathcalD(\cdot)$ that takes a set, and "expands" it to give us the set of all possible distributions on that set.

series-probability-theory-channels::42.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::42.snippetHtml: Then a channel from $X$ to $Y$ is a function $f\to \mathcalD(Y)$, which you might also see written $f: X\klarrow Y$. For each point in $X$, $f$ maps it to a single point in $\mathcalD(Y)$, like a function must – but that single point refers to a whole distribution over the points of $Y$.

series-probability-theory-channels::43.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::43.snippetHtml: Consider this channel from a two-element source to a two-element target:

series-probability-theory-channels::45.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::45.snippetHtml: Here's how we could draw this channel as a function that respects the rules:

series-probability-theory-channels::46.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::46.snippetHtml: Probabilities are real numbers. There are infinitely many real numbers. It doesn't matter that our target $Y$ has only two points in this case—we need to assign a real number to each of them, so there's an uncountably infinite number of distributions on our target. We've skipped over most of them in the diagram above, with the help of some dots.

series-probability-theory-channels::47.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::47.snippetHtml: There is one other way we could show this in a diagram. For each point (distribution) in $\mathcalD(Y)$ there are two real numbers (probabilities). They must add up to $1$, so we only need to remember one of them – if I know one is 0.6, the other one must of course be 0.4. So we could draw a diagram that maps to just one real number for each point in $X$ – say, the probability of arriving at $y_1$.

series-probability-theory-channels::49.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::49.snippetHtml: These two diagrams may be more formally correct than the multi-arrow diagrams we'll use, but I don't think they're as intuitive – and they'll quickly get ugly, when the source and target sets have more than two members.

series-probability-theory-channels::50.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::50.snippetHtml: We'll keep breaking the rules, and draw our channels with multiple arrows starting from the same source point. While it's informal and "wrong", visually it'll be nice because it shows how a channel is a collection of hypotheses about how different outcomes lead to each other.

series-probability-theory-channels::51.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::51.snippetHtml: Suppose we're asking questions about a specific disease. There's a set $\mathsf{D}$ which has two points: does someone have the disease ($d\mathsf{+}$), or don't they ($d\mathsf{-}$)? And there's another set $\mathsf{T}$, also with two points: does that person test positive for the disease ($t+$), or not ($t-$)?

series-probability-theory-channels::52.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::52.snippetHtml: A channel that connects $\mathsfD$ to $\mathsfT$ describes how strongly we believe in the different ways this test can turn out.

series-probability-theory-channels::54.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::54.snippetHtml: If the person really has the disease, our channel here says the test will probably be positive—this is the large arrow labeled T pos., for true positive. And that's good, since we want the truth about whether they're infected!

series-probability-theory-channels::55.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::55.snippetHtml: But there's some small chance that the test will fail, and tell us falsely that someone with the disease is actually disease-free. That's the false negative case.

series-probability-theory-channels::56.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::56.snippetHtml: When someone doesn't actually have the disease, there are also the true negative and false positive arrows.

series-probability-theory-channels::57.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::57.snippetHtml: That diagram shows one example of a channel from $\mathsfD$ to $\mathsfT$, with specific probabilities. It describes a pretty good test, that usually gives accurate results. To describe a badly-designed test that usually gives a positive result, even when the disease is absent, we could write a different channel with a thick F pos. arrow.

series-probability-theory-channels::58.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::58.snippetHtml: And in a better world, maybe our tests would be perfectly accurate. That'd look like this:

series-probability-theory-channels::60.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::60.snippetHtml: We're back to where we started: a channel with all its weight on one arrow per starting point is just a simple function!

series-probability-theory-channels::62.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::62.snippetHtml: This isn't a useful model of the way disease tests actually work. Real tests aren't always reliable, just like (sadly) Max doesn't always roll ones.

series-probability-theory-channels::63.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::63.snippetHtml: The classic way of writing down a value from a conditional probability distribution uses the $p(\cdot)$ notation.

series-probability-theory-channels::64.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::64.snippetHtml: For example, if there's a 90% probability of T pos., we can write $p_{~\mathsf{T}|\mathsf{D}~}(t\mathsf{+}~|~d\mathsf{+})=0.9$, or simply $p(t\mathsf{+}~|~d\mathsf{+})=0.9$.

series-probability-theory-channels::65.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::65.snippetHtml: Here's another way we could write this, using functional notation we've already seen: $p(d\mathsf{+}\mapsto t\mathsf{+})=0.9$.

series-probability-theory-channels::67.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::67.snippetHtml: Say we have two channels, and the target of the first channel is the same as the source of the second channel.

series-probability-theory-channels::69.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::69.snippetHtml: These can be glued together to form a composite that – like a composite of simple functions – forgets what happens in between.

series-probability-theory-channels::70.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::70.snippetHtml: The weighted arrows make it easy to see which individual paths are followed often (like $x_2\mapsto y_1 \mapsto z_2$) and which aren't ($x_1\mapsto y_1 \mapsto z_1$).

series-probability-theory-channels::71.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::71.snippetHtml: To get the composite, we collapse all the paths that go from one point in the source, to one point in the target. For example, here are the paths that get collapsed to form the arrow $x_1\mapsto z_1$:

series-probability-theory-channels::73.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::73.snippetHtml: Even though there's a low chance of following the path $x_1\mapsto y_1 \mapsto z_1$, there's still a decent chance of following the composite arrow $x_1\mapsto z_1$ because we could also have reached $z_1$ through $y_2$ or $y_3$.

series-probability-theory-channels::74.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::74.snippetHtml: Paths get collapsed according to this rule: multiply along, then sum across.

series-probability-theory-channels::75.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::75.snippetHtml: First, multiply along: if there's a $10%$ chance I'll reach $y_1$ from $x_1$, and then a $20%$ chance I'll reach $z_1$ from $y_1$, then there's only a $10%\times20%=2%$ chance I'll reach $z_1$ from $x_1$.

series-probability-theory-channels::76.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::76.snippetHtml: Then sum across: there are actually three paths from $x_1$ to $z_1$. After repeating the multiplication step for each path, we sum the results together.

series-probability-theory-channels::77.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::77.snippetHtml: If we have a channel $f\to \mathcalD(Y)$ and a channel $g\to \mathcalD(Z)$, their composite is given by

series-probability-theory-channels::79.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::79.snippetHtml: A channel gives a distribution on (not just a point in) $Y$ for each point in $X$. So $f(x_1)$ refers to an entire distribution, and $f(x_1)(y_1)$ picks out one probability from that distribution: the probability of reaching $y_1$ given that we started from $x_1$.

series-probability-theory-channels::80.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::80.snippetHtml: We use the notation $\ccomp$ instead of $\comp$ to make it clear that we're composing channels $f\to\mathcalD(Y)$ and not simple functions $f\to Y$.

series-probability-theory-channels::81.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::81.snippetHtml: Note that the equation is a sum of products. In our example above, if we label the channels $g$ and $f$, we can write this out as

series-probability-theory-channels::83.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::83.snippetHtml: If you've studied linear algebra, this might look familiar: it's the inner (or "dot") product of two vectors.

series-probability-theory-channels::84.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::84.snippetHtml: Actually, we can represent our channels as matrices. Then the matrix for the composite channel is obtained by matrix multiplication

series-probability-theory-channels::86.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::86.snippetHtml: And our calculation for the single arrow $x_1\mapsto z_1$ corresponds to the product of a single row with a single column.

series-probability-theory-channels::88.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::88.snippetHtml: Note that matrix multiplication uses the "last step appears first" ordering, similarly to $g\ccomp f$.

series-probability-theory-channels::89.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::89.snippetHtml: In more traditional notation, we could write:

series-probability-theory-channels::91.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::91.snippetHtml: The string diagram for channel composition looks essentially identical to that for function composition.

series-probability-theory-channels::93.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::93.snippetHtml: When using string diagrams, because they are abstract, it's important to be clear about the type of objects we're working with. On the left hand side of this diagram, are $f$ and $g$ simple functions, or are they channels? In this series, by default the objects shown in our string diagrams will be channels, of which (as we've seen) simple functions are a special case.

series-probability-theory-channels::95.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::95.snippetHtml: Last time, we saw that under certain conditions, we can invert a function $\mathsfX\to\mathsfY$ to get a function $\mathsfY\to\mathsfX$. Can we do the same with our channel?

series-probability-theory-channels::96.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::96.snippetHtml: It turns out the situation is not as straightforward as it was with simple functions.

series-probability-theory-channels::97.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::97.snippetHtml: If there's an $6%$ chance I'll reach $y_1$ from $x_1$, and a $33%$ chance I'll reach $y_1$ from $x_2$, what are the inverted probabilities I'll reach $x_1$ from $y_1$, and $x_2$ from $y_1$?

series-probability-theory-channels::98.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::98.snippetHtml: Before we can calculate that, we'll need a little more information. Specifically, we'll need the probability that we had started from each point in $\mathsfX$ in the first place. Our channel doesn't tell us that—it only tells us the probability that we would arrive at a certain point in $\mathsfY$, given that we'd started from a certain point in $\mathsfX$. Consider: if we actually start from $x_1$ $100%$ of the time, and never from $x_2$, does it make sense to say that we'd ever arrive back at $x_2$, once we reverse the arrows?

series-probability-theory-channels::99.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::99.snippetHtml: Like with simple functions, we can run into the problem of unfollowed paths when trying to invert channels: when the probability of an arrow is zero, we never follow it – so we can't invert it.

series-probability-theory-channels::100.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::100.snippetHtml: Different from a simple function, a channel could reach any target point from any source point. And the only time we absolutely have no information about how to go backwards, is when all of the arrows arriving at a given target point have zero probability.

series-probability-theory-channels::101.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::101.snippetHtml: The solution to this problem is called Bayes' theorem, and we'll come back to it in a later post.

series-probability-theory-channels::102.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::102.snippetHtml: It will be extremely useful. We already have a channel that tells us how likely we are to test positive or negative for a disease, given that we have it or not. Bayes' theorem will let us invert it, to get a channel that tells us how likely we are to have the disease or not, given that we test positive or negative – which in practice is the information we usually need.

series-probability-theory-channels::104.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::104.snippetHtml: The usual way that probability is taught, channels are called conditional probability distributions. Their functional nature is by no means neglected, but it does fade into the background much of the time.

series-probability-theory-channels::105.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::105.snippetHtml: On the other hand, it's very common for an experienced researcher to write $p(y~|~x)$ for a value in a conditional distribution, intuitively aware that they're talking about something function-like that starts from values of $\mathsfX$ and reaches distributions over $\mathsfY$.

series-probability-theory-channels::106.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::106.snippetHtml: Here, we've kept functions in the foreground since the beginning. Taking this view, channels aren't just one more tool we'll use for probability. They are the atoms of the theory – its moving parts – and almost all of our tools will be special cases of channels and their composition.

series-probability-theory-channels::107.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::107.snippetHtml: Next, we'll see two of these special cases – and the fundamentally dual roles they serve.

series-probability-theory-channels::108.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::108.snippetHtml: Conditional distributions are also the central feature of the theory of Bayesian networks. Much of what we discuss in this series could be framed as a re-telling of that theory.

series-probability-theory-channels::109.title: Channels (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-channels::109.snippetHtml: "Edge" rather than "channel". When we're discussing graph structures formed by multiple channels, it may be convenient to refer to those channels as edges. But in general, I think channel has a clearer flavour of the flow of causality or information.

series-probability-theory-events::0.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::0.snippetHtml: Last time, we learned about the basic building block of our theory: the channel, or conditional probability distribution. Now we'll learn about two special cases of this which we'll use often enough that they'll get special names and representations:

series-probability-theory-events::1.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::1.snippetHtml: • States are plain old "probability distributions". The unconditional ones.

series-probability-theory-events::2.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::2.snippetHtml: States are plain old "probability distributions". The unconditional ones.

series-probability-theory-events::3.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::3.snippetHtml: • Events are statements or observations about outcomes.

series-probability-theory-events::4.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::4.snippetHtml: Events are statements or observations about outcomes.

series-probability-theory-events::5.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::5.snippetHtml: Functionally, events and states have opposite roles and flavours.

series-probability-theory-events::7.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::7.snippetHtml: A channel gives a distribution on the target, for every point we could start from in the source. But where do we start from?

series-probability-theory-events::8.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::8.snippetHtml: The disease→test channel we saw last time gives us the probability that someone will get a certain test result, conditional that they have the disease or not.

series-probability-theory-events::10.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::10.snippetHtml: How many positive tests do we actually expect to see, in practice? That depends on how many people actually have the disease. Simply, unconditionally, with nothing left to be given.

series-probability-theory-events::11.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::11.snippetHtml: There's a specific kind of channel we can use for that: a channel that starts from a set that has only one point in it.

series-probability-theory-events::12.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::12.snippetHtml: We don't need to label that one point. There are no other options to distinguish it from. It's always given. We always start from it.

series-probability-theory-events::13.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::13.snippetHtml: This kind of channel is called a state, because it models a given state of the world.

series-probability-theory-events::14.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::14.snippetHtml: This state on $\mathsfD$ gives the probability that someone will have the disease, without the answer depending on any other context.

series-probability-theory-events::15.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::15.snippetHtml: • A channel, or a conditional (probability) distribution, is a collection of distributions/states on a target set, where we haven't decided yet which distribution is given.

series-probability-theory-events::16.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::16.snippetHtml: A channel, or a conditional (probability) distribution, is a collection of distributions/states on a target set, where we haven't decided yet which distribution is given.

series-probability-theory-events::17.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::17.snippetHtml: • A state is a single distribution on a target set. This is traditionally just called a (probability) distribution.

series-probability-theory-events::18.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::18.snippetHtml: A state is a single distribution on a target set. This is traditionally just called a (probability) distribution.

series-probability-theory-events::19.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::19.snippetHtml: Compared to states, channels have an extra qualifier ("conditional") in their traditional names. This might lead us to think that channels are a special case, when really it's the other way around! </InfoCallout>

series-probability-theory-events::20.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::20.snippetHtml: For example, perhaps we have a prior belief in a 1% probability of having the disease, because that's what we've observed over a long time. But maybe we live in Norway and we've only been observing Norwegians. Or maybe a surprise pandemic will happen next year.

series-probability-theory-events::21.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::21.snippetHtml: The important thing is that making a probability distribution unconditional on anything else is a convenience, for the sake of modeling a particular situation. If the context changes, our model may also have to change.

series-probability-theory-events::22.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::22.snippetHtml: Later in this post we'll learn about one way we can update our prior beliefs, given new information.

series-probability-theory-events::23.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::23.snippetHtml: In the previous post, we already saw an example of something that looks like a state.

series-probability-theory-events::25.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::25.snippetHtml: By excluding the other members of the source set, we were saying something like "we've decided Max is the one rolling dice now". In that sense, we were narrowing the context for our model. We could have focused on Claire instead. *Any* channel can be seen as a collection of states, one for each point in the source that we might start from, or decide is "given". </InfoCallout>

series-probability-theory-events::27.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::27.snippetHtml: [Jacobs *et al.*](/series/probability-theory#sources) use the *ket* notation $\ket{\cdot}$ to write out states. For example:

series-probability-theory-events::29.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::29.snippetHtml: The terms $\ketx_i$ are not numbers. They're the points on which the distribution is defined. So $r_i\ketx_i$ does not imply actual multiplication. The equation means "I'll take $r_1$ of point $x_1$, and $r_2$ of point $x_2$, and ..., to form my state on $X$."

series-probability-theory-events::30.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::30.snippetHtml: For example, a state describing a fair coin looks like

series-probability-theory-events::32.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::32.snippetHtml: A state is a special type of channel, but we can also see *any* channel $f\to \mathcal{D}(Y)$ as a set of states. For each point $x$ in the channel's source $X$, there is one state on $Y$, $\omega_{x}:\mathbf{1}\to \mathcal{D}(Y)$. </NotationCallout>

series-probability-theory-events::34.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::34.snippetHtml: So, what's the overall probability of a positive test?

series-probability-theory-events::35.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::35.snippetHtml: A state is just a type of channel, and we can compose it with other channels. That's how we can transform our state on $\mathsfD$ to a state on $\mathsfT$.

series-probability-theory-events::37.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::37.snippetHtml: The thickness of the bottom path $\boldsymbol{\cA{\to}\cC{\to}}$ makes it clear that almost all the time, the person being tested doesn't actually have the disease, and the test accurately reports that they don't: we'll see mostly negative tests.

series-probability-theory-events::38.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::38.snippetHtml: The probability of a positive test is about $7%$, though the probability of having the disease was only $2%$. That's because there are two paths that reach a positive test.

series-probability-theory-events::40.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::40.snippetHtml: There's only a $\cA{2\%}$ chance we'll have the disease, and in that case we'll test positive $\cB{90}\%$ of the time – so $\cA{2\%}\cZ\times\cB{90\%}\cZ=1.8\%$ of the time, we follow the upper path to a positive test . But there's also a $\cC 5\%$ chance the test will be a false positive, in the $\cA{98\%}$ of cases where we don't have the disease. We follow the lower path $\cA{98\%}\cZ\times\cC{5\%}\cZ=4.9\%$ of the time. Most of the positive tests are actually false positives!

series-probability-theory-events::42.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::42.snippetHtml: However, because states hold a privileged position as unconditional channels, state transformation deserves some special notation. Here are two alternatives for writing the composite:

series-probability-theory-events::43.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::43.snippetHtml: • with a function: $\sigma = f_*(\omega)$ The asterisk makes it clear that $\omega$ is not an input $x\in X$ to $f$ – it's an entire distribution on $\mathcalD(X)$ that's pushed through $f$.

series-probability-theory-events::44.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::44.snippetHtml: with a function: $\sigma = f_*(\omega)$ The asterisk makes it clear that $\omega$ is not an input $x\in X$ to $f$ – it's an entire distribution on $\mathcalD(X)$ that's pushed through $f$.

series-probability-theory-events::45.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::45.snippetHtml: • with an operator: $\sigma = f \gg \omega$ In this case, $\gg$ is essentially a direct substitute for $\ccomp$ that emphasizes that this is a pushforward composition.

series-probability-theory-events::46.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::46.snippetHtml: with an operator: $\sigma = f \gg \omega$ In this case, $\gg$ is essentially a direct substitute for $\ccomp$ that emphasizes that this is a pushforward composition.

series-probability-theory-events::49.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::49.snippetHtml: This morning, I was still half-asleep when I wandered to my fridge to get something to drink. There were three options: coffee with milk, decaffeinated coffee with milk, and a coffee-flavoured protein shake. (I enjoy variety.)

series-probability-theory-events::50.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::50.snippetHtml: Now it's 30 minutes later, and I can't remember which one I drank. I was half-asleep, and they all taste pretty similar.

series-probability-theory-events::51.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::51.snippetHtml: Normally, I'd reach for the coffee ($b_\mathsfc$) about 80% of the time, but only 10% each for the decaf ($b_\mathsfd$) or the protein shake ($b_\mathsfp$). These prior beliefs can be represented by a state.

series-probability-theory-events::53.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::53.snippetHtml: An event is a statement, the answer to a true-false question, about a set of outcomes. Here are two events that are relevant to our current problem:

series-probability-theory-events::54.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::54.snippetHtml: On the left, we map the protein shake and the decaf coffee to $\mathsfT$ (for $\mathsfTrue$) because they satisfy the claim "this lacks caffeine".

series-probability-theory-events::55.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::55.snippetHtml: On the right, we see the opposite: only the coffee is mapped to $\mathsfT$, in answer to "this has caffeine".

series-probability-theory-events::56.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::56.snippetHtml: These two events are mutually exclusive, since one can't happen when the other does: either we drank something that has caffeine, or something that doesn't.

series-probability-theory-events::58.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::58.snippetHtml: Like states, events are also a special type of channel.

series-probability-theory-events::59.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::59.snippetHtml: We just saw an event $\mathsf{Lacks~caffeine}$, which is a simple function. [Recall](/series/probability-theory/channels#functions-are-channels) that simple functions are a special case of channels where all the weight is on one arrow for each starting point. That means we can re-draw our $\mathsf{Lacks~caffeine}$ event as such a channel.

series-probability-theory-events::61.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::61.snippetHtml: Finally, since there are only two ending points ($\mathsfT$ and $\mathsfF$), and each starting point must form a distribution over them that sums to 1 (or 100%), we really only need to remember one of the two probabilities.

series-probability-theory-events::63.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::63.snippetHtml: We can imagine events that are only *kind of* true or false, by giving weights between 0 and 1. For instance, we said our $\mathsf{Has~caffeine}$ event was all-or-nothing: the coffee maps to 1, and the other two drinks map to 0. But a decaf coffee still has a trace amount of caffeine, maybe around 3% of a regular coffee. We could model that as a *fuzzy* event instead:

series-probability-theory-events::64.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::64.snippetHtml: Why might fuzzy events be useful? Well, information can be unreliable, and statements about the world (not just beliefs about states of the world) can be uncertain. Fuzziness allows us to represent that.

series-probability-theory-events::68.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::68.snippetHtml:
• A sharp (non-fuzzy) event $E\subseteq A$: $\mathbf1_E$

    • $\mathbf1A$ and $\mathbf0=\mathbf1\emptyset$ for the truth-falsity (all/nothing) events

series-probability-theory-events::86.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::86.snippetHtml: When fuzzy events are allowed, we can pull an event back through a channel, similarly to how we were able to push a state forward.

series-probability-theory-events::87.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::87.snippetHtml: This doesn't work if we want to use only non-fuzzy, all-or-nothing events: if we pull a non-fuzzy event back through a channel, we generally get a fuzzy one!

series-probability-theory-events::88.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::88.snippetHtml: This is yet another example of channel composition.

series-probability-theory-events::89.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::89.snippetHtml: For example, this is how we would pull back the event $\mathsf{Receives~care}$ in the disease network. Depending on how positive or negative test results determine whether care is received or not, $\mathsf{Receives~care}$ corresponds to a fuzzy event stating whether the test is positive or negative. In turn, that corresponds to a fuzzy event stating whether the patient has the disease.

series-probability-theory-events::91.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::91.snippetHtml: We could write this event transformation in two ways:

series-probability-theory-events::96.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::96.snippetHtml: In the preceding three diagrams, the respective events could be labeled as follows: $\mathbf{1}_{\{c\}}$, then $\mathrm{g}^*\left(\mathbf{1}_{\{c\}}\right)$, then $\mathrm{f}^*\left(\mathrm{g}^*\left(\mathbf{1}_{\{c\}}\right)\right)$.

series-probability-theory-events::98.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::98.snippetHtml: Given my usual chances of drinking each thing, what's the probability I drank something without caffeine?

series-probability-theory-events::100.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::100.snippetHtml: This is just another case of composition – multiply along, sum across. We're specifically interested in the probability we'll end at $\mathsfT$, so let's calculate just that part.

series-probability-theory-events::102.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::102.snippetHtml: Since the event is a function, each of its arrows ($\boldsymbol{\cB\to}$,$\boldsymbol{\cC\to}$) has weight $1$, or $100\%$. That means nothing happens when we multiply along each path, and we can just sum over the blue arrows:

series-probability-theory-events::104.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::104.snippetHtml: This might seem pretty obvious: I had a 10% chance of drinking each of the two caffeine-free drinks, so there's a 20% chance I drank something caffeine-free.

series-probability-theory-events::105.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::105.snippetHtml: More generally, we can compute the probability, or validity of a fuzzy event by composing it with a state, to get a fuzzy predicate with a single arrow, i.e. a statement of a single probability.

series-probability-theory-events::106.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::106.snippetHtml: This probability operation can be seen as both an event transformation (pulling back the event $E$ onto the single-element set, treating the state as a channel) and as a state transformation (pushing forward the state $\omega$ onto $\left{ \mathsfT, \mathsfF \right}$, treating the event as a channel). In classic probability theory, $E$ is only ever a non-fuzzy/sharp event.

series-probability-theory-events::107.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::107.snippetHtml: We use a different notation for validity, writing $\omega\models p$, and adopting the following:

series-probability-theory-events::120.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::120.snippetHtml: • Note this is syntactic sugar for a special kind of channel composition

series-probability-theory-events::121.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::121.snippetHtml: Note this is syntactic sugar for a special kind of channel composition

series-probability-theory-events::122.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::122.snippetHtml: For mathematicians, logicians, and computer scientists the symbol $\models$ has some prior meaning: $A\models B$ means that $B$ is a semantic consequence of $A$, or that a less general structure $B$ satisfies a more general structure $A$. So, how much does an event satisfy a state of affairs?

series-probability-theory-events::123.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::123.snippetHtml: For others, this notation is kind of unfortunate. The symbol $\models$ is visually similar to the equals sign $=$, which makes it harder to visually chunk equations without including extra parentheses.

series-probability-theory-events::125.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::125.snippetHtml: It's also kind of similar to symbols sometimes used in probability theory for conditional dependence $\conddep$ and independence $\condindep$

series-probability-theory-events::126.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::126.snippetHtml: What could be an alternative? I'm no mathematician, but how about $\omega\parallel p$? In geometry, $AB \parallel CD$ means "the line $AB$ is parallel to the line $CD$". Maybe it's a valid to consider how "aligned" an event is with a state of affairs, especially considering that the calculation of validity is analogous to a dot product between vectors.

series-probability-theory-events::127.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::127.snippetHtml: Consider the same equations as above, written with this operator:

series-probability-theory-events::140.snippetHtml: What are the disadvantages of this notation?

series-probability-theory-events::141.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::141.snippetHtml: • it might be mistaken for ||, which is a common programming syntax for the logical OR operator. But there's already largely a separation between mathematical and programming notation.
