series-probability-theory-events::143.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::143.snippetHtml: • the notation for conditioning, which we'll introduce in a moment, uses a single vertical line, which in combination with $\parallel$ could also lead to some chunking issues.

series-probability-theory-events::144.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::144.snippetHtml: the notation for conditioning, which we'll introduce in a moment, uses a single vertical line, which in combination with $\parallel$ could also lead to some chunking issues.

series-probability-theory-events::145.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::145.snippetHtml: While it might not be absolutely wise to introduce new notation in the first place, it does happen sometimes. As long as the notation is not super well-established (such as is the case with $\models$) it's worth discussing how it affects the user experience. </NotationCallout>

series-probability-theory-events::147.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::147.snippetHtml: While states and fuzzy events are both special types of channels, they have different properties and serve different roles.

series-probability-theory-events::148.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::148.snippetHtml: • States are more ontological (world model / prior beliefs) whereas events are more epistemic (statements or observations).

series-probability-theory-events::149.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::149.snippetHtml: States are more ontological (world model / prior beliefs) whereas events are more epistemic (statements or observations).

series-probability-theory-events::150.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::150.snippetHtml: • States must be consistent (distributional) whereas events are potentially inconsistent (not distributional). There's nothing stopping us from having a fuzzy event that maps $d+$ to 0.6, and $d-$ to 0.8

series-probability-theory-events::151.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::151.snippetHtml: States must be consistent (distributional) whereas events are potentially inconsistent (not distributional). There's nothing stopping us from having a fuzzy event that maps $d+$ to 0.6, and $d-$ to 0.8

series-probability-theory-events::152.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::152.snippetHtml: • State information moves forwards through the network of channels, and represent causality. Event information moves backwards and represents the influence of epistemic context.

series-probability-theory-events::153.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::153.snippetHtml: State information moves forwards through the network of channels, and represent causality. Event information moves backwards and represents the influence of epistemic context.

series-probability-theory-events::154.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::154.snippetHtml: Basically, this looks like treating the fuzzy event as a channel $X\klarrow \mathbf{2}$, where $\mathbf{2}=\lbrace t,f\rbrace$. Then the original fuzzy event can be recovered by pulling back $\mathbf{1}_{\lbrace t\rbrace}$ through that channel.

series-probability-theory-events::155.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::155.snippetHtml: Since fuzzy events are actually a special type of channel, there's no reason in principle that we can't do this, modeling the fuzziness of the event as just another part of the network of state-transforming channels.

series-probability-theory-events::156.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::156.snippetHtml: However, from the functional perspective, it does seem like a hack because it does not preserve what's important about the duality between states and events. Remember, all-or-nothing events can't be transformed backwards through the channels in a network, to get all-or-nothing events on preceding nodes. On the other hand, fuzzy events are closed under this operation. </InfoCallout>

series-probability-theory-events::157.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::157.snippetHtml: • A state $\omega\in\mathcalD(X)$ can also be seen as a function $X\rightarrow[0,1]$. Thus a state is also a fuzzy event.

series-probability-theory-events::158.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::158.snippetHtml: A state $\omega\in\mathcalD(X)$ can also be seen as a function $X\rightarrow[0,1]$. Thus a state is also a fuzzy event.

series-probability-theory-events::159.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::159.snippetHtml: - However, a fuzzy event $p: X\rightarrow[0,1]$ does not in general form a state, since it may be the case that $\sum_{x\in X} p(x) \neq 1$. A fuzzy event is not a distribution.

series-probability-theory-events::160.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::160.snippetHtml: However, a fuzzy event $p: X\rightarrow[0,1]$ does not in general form a state, since it may be the case that $\sum_{x\in X} p(x) \neq 1$. A fuzzy event is not a distribution.

series-probability-theory-events::161.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::161.snippetHtml: • The set of states $\mathcalD(X)$ forms a convex set, but the set of fuzzy events $[0,1]^X$ forms an effect module.

series-probability-theory-events::162.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::162.snippetHtml: The set of states $\mathcalD(X)$ forms a convex set, but the set of fuzzy events $[0,1]^X$ forms an effect module.

series-probability-theory-events::164.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::164.snippetHtml: Earlier I claimed a 20% chance I drank something caffeine-free, based on my prior knowledge of how I usually behave. That's fine… but based on how I'm feeling now, I'm sure that what I drank didn't have caffeine in it. In that case, clearly the chance that I drank one of the two caffeine-free drinks isn't just 20%. Intuitively, it should actually be 100%: 50% for the protein shake, and 50% for the decaf coffee, since we've eliminated the 80% chance that what I drank was the regular coffee.

series-probability-theory-events::165.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::165.snippetHtml: The calculation we just intuitively described is conditioning: if I know that a certain event has occurred in a given context, I can use that information to update a state to suit the context.[^4]

series-probability-theory-events::166.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::166.snippetHtml: I know I drank something with no caffeine. How does that affect the prior state on $\mathsfB$?

series-probability-theory-events::169.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::169.snippetHtml: For each point $a\in A$, we multiply the probability $\omega(a)$ given by the state by the weight $p(a)$ given to $a$ by the predicate, then renormalize by the validity $\omega\parallel p$. Even if the validity of $p$ given $\omega$ is only 5%, conditioning assumes we are "in" this 5%, which is why we divide by it. This also means conditioning on $p$ and on any rescaled version $r\cdot p$ ($r\neq 0$) gives the same result.

series-probability-theory-events::172.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::172.snippetHtml: Note on notation: the classical $\Pr(B|A)$ is misleading because $B|A$ is not an event, and the vertical bar looks like it should be an operator. The two-step view (update, then evaluate) makes the structure explicit. </NotationCallout>

series-probability-theory-events::174.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::174.snippetHtml: Two calculations are happening here, but they aren't the same two we've described. We can re-derive the classical formula in terms of conditioning and validity. Using sharp events $\mathbf1_A$ and $\mathbf1_B$ on a state $\omega$:

series-probability-theory-events::176.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::176.snippetHtml: The last expression reads: condition $\omega$ on $\mathbf{1}_A$, then take the validity of $\mathbf{1}_B$. This generalizes naturally to fuzzy predicates: $\omega\rvert_p\parallel q$. </NotationCallout>

series-probability-theory-events::177.title: States and events (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-events::177.snippetHtml: [^4]: This depends on the state and the event being defined on the same set of outcomes, just like channel composition only works when the target of the first channel is the same as the source of the second one, so they fit together.

series-probability-theory-functions::0.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::0.snippetHtml: My friends and I are playing a game, and we have a problem. We need to flip a coin, but we haven't got one.

series-probability-theory-functions::1.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::1.snippetHtml: There's an app we could use instead – but let's be creative.

series-probability-theory-functions::2.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::2.snippetHtml: We do happen to have some six-sided dice. If we come up with the right kind of rule, dice rolls will work like coin tosses.

series-probability-theory-functions::3.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::3.snippetHtml: Let's say the numbers 1, 2, and 3 count as $\mathsfheads$, while 4, 5, and 6 count as $\mathsftails$.

series-probability-theory-functions::5.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::5.snippetHtml: Other, similar rules would work just as well.

series-probability-theory-functions::7.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::7.snippetHtml: Say we stick with one such rule, where half the numbers map to heads, the other half to tails. And our dice rolls are fair: each number from 1 to 6 comes up just as often as each of the others. In that case we'll reach $\mathsfheads$ on half our rolls, and $\mathsftails$ on the other half.

series-probability-theory-functions::8.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::8.snippetHtml: We've found a way to use fair dice rolls as a model of fair coin flips.[^7]

series-probability-theory-functions::10.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::10.snippetHtml: Our rule that converts dice rolls to coin flips is an example of a function.

series-probability-theory-functions::11.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::11.snippetHtml: What makes something a function? Let's get a little more abstract for just a second. Here's a function called $f$ that doesn't have to do with coins, or dice, or anything in particular:

series-probability-theory-functions::13.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::13.snippetHtml: A function is just a way to start from one set of things, and reach another set. Here, we start from points in $\mathsfX$ and arrive at points in $\mathsfY$.[^6] The points in $\mathsfX$ can also be called elements or members of $\mathsfX$.

series-probability-theory-functions::14.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::14.snippetHtml: No matter where we start in our source, a function must give us only one place to go in our target. In the current example, exactly one arrow needs to start at each of the three points in $\mathsfX$, and end somewhere in $\mathsfY$.

series-probability-theory-functions::15.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::15.snippetHtml: We already saw two different functions, that transform fair dice rolls into fair coin tosses. The source set represented the six sides of the dice, so each function had six arrows.

series-probability-theory-functions::16.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::16.snippetHtml: A function $f: X\rightarrow Y$ starts from points in the source set $X$, and goes to points in the target set $Y$. We write $f(x)=y$ to say "the function $f$ reaches $y$ when it starts from $x$", or "when given the input data $x$, $f$ transforms it into the output data $y$".

series-probability-theory-functions::17.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::17.snippetHtml: Because $f$ is a function, when we write $f\rightarrow Y$, we're saying that for every $x\in X$, there is exactly one $y\in Y$ for which $f(x)=y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::18.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::18.snippetHtml: In mathematics, the plain arrow "$\rightarrow$" is generally used to indicate the source and target of an entire function, like it is in the notation $f: X\rightarrow Y$. (If you hear a mathematician talking about "an arrow", this is probably the kind of arrow they mean.) This isn't the same kind of arrow as the arrows in our diagrams so far, which start from just one point in $X$ and reach just one point in $Y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::19.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::19.snippetHtml: The arrows shown in our mapping diagrams are actually the ones inside a function. These are normally written down like $f: x \mapsto y$, which says the same thing as $f(x)=y$. For example, for the function in the previous mapping diagram:

series-probability-theory-functions::20.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::20.snippetHtml: $$f: x_1\mapsto y_1~~~\mathrmor~~~f(x_1)=y_1$$ $$f: x_2\mapsto y_2~~~\mathrmor~~~f(x_2)=y_2$$ $$f: x_3\mapsto y_2~~~\mathrmor~~~f(x_3)=y_3$$

series-probability-theory-functions::21.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::21.snippetHtml: Bringing the two kinds of arrows together: when we write $f: X\to Y$, we mean that for every $x\in X$, there is some $y\in Y$ so that $f\mapsto y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::22.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::22.snippetHtml: String diagrams are a more visual way of writing equations that are just as formal as traditional notation.

series-probability-theory-functions::23.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::23.snippetHtml: If we forget about all the arrows inside our function $f\to Y$, we could collapse our last mapping diagram down into something like this:

series-probability-theory-functions::25.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::25.snippetHtml: The string diagram for $f\to Y$ shows the same information, but it emphasizes the function instead of the source and target sets:

series-probability-theory-functions::27.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::27.snippetHtml: Note that the arrows have become boxes, and the boxes have become wires.

series-probability-theory-functions::28.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::28.snippetHtml: String diagrams are often written bottom-to-top, but we'll write them left-to-right.

series-probability-theory-functions::29.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::29.snippetHtml: If the number of arrows doesn't match the size of the source set, it's not a function.

series-probability-theory-functions::31.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::31.snippetHtml: These aren't functions. The one on the left has too few arrows – where do we go from $x_3$? The one on the right has too many – if we start at $x_2$, do we go to $y_1$ or $y_2$?

series-probability-theory-functions::32.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::32.snippetHtml: Importantly, a function doesn't need to reach everywhere in the target. More than one of its arrows can end in the same place.

series-probability-theory-functions::34.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::34.snippetHtml: $\mathsfX$ and $\mathsfY$ aren't the only source and target we could choose. Say we choose a target with three points (like $\mathsfY$) but a source with only two points (unlike $\mathsfX$). In that case, how many ways are there to draw a function?

series-probability-theory-functions::36.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::36.snippetHtml: We don't need to label the sets or their points, to show all the ways we can follow the rules. Any time we have a source set with two things in it, no matter what they are, and we want to choose a function that reaches a target set with three things in it, no matter what they are, those are the 9 different mappings – combinations of arrows – we could possibly choose.

series-probability-theory-functions::37.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::37.snippetHtml: Say we have a target set with $M$ elements. A function contains one arrow for each element in the source, with $M$ possible choices about where that arrow should reach. So if the source set has two elements, then there's a total of $M\times M$ (or, $M^2$) functions we could choose. And if the source set has $N$ elements, then there are $M^N$ possible functions.

series-probability-theory-functions::38.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::38.snippetHtml: Dice have six sides and a coin has two, so there are $2^6=64$ rules we could choose about how to turn dice rolls into coin flips. That also includes the "unfair" rules, though. For example, one of those rules turns all six sides into heads, which is probably not a rule we want to choose if we are trying to model a coin flip. Of the 64 rules we could choose, only $\binom63=20$ of them are fair.

series-probability-theory-functions::39.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::39.snippetHtml: Some of those mappings make more sense than others, depending on the meaning we give to the members of the sets we want to map between.

series-probability-theory-functions::41.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::41.snippetHtml: The one on the left is clearly more valid, given the usual behaviour of cats and dogs. But what if we choose a different source set with the same size?

series-probability-theory-functions::43.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::43.snippetHtml: Humans may be omnivorous in general, but unless you know Max and Claire already, you probably can't say which of these describes their habits better.

series-probability-theory-functions::44.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::44.snippetHtml: We can choose any source and any target, and any possible function that goes between them, depending on our purposes. At the start of this post, we wanted to turn a dice roll into a coin flip. In our last two examples, we tried to show something about the diets of some creatures.

series-probability-theory-functions::45.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::45.snippetHtml: Once we decide on the sets, the possible ways we can draw arrows only depends on the size of the source and the size of the target.

series-probability-theory-functions::46.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::46.snippetHtml: Our comparison between the diagrams for $\mathsfcats$-$\mathsfdogs$ versus $\mathsfMax$-$\mathsfClaire$ is an example of a difference between syntax and semantics.

series-probability-theory-functions::47.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::47.snippetHtml: Roughly speaking, syntax is the way we write things down. In terms of arrows, the two diagrams are written the same way. However, the meaning or semantics of the two diagrams is clearly different.

series-probability-theory-functions::48.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::48.snippetHtml: Of course, people don't usually draw diagrams just because they want to remember things about people, or make rules about games. But as we move forward in this series, drawing diagrams like these will help us to understand probability in terms of following paths between collections of possibilities.

series-probability-theory-functions::50.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::50.snippetHtml: Why do my friends and I need to flip a coin for our game?

series-probability-theory-functions::51.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::51.snippetHtml: Because the next player only gets to move if it comes up heads!

series-probability-theory-functions::53.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::53.snippetHtml: This is also a function, and it fits together with our function from earlier.

series-probability-theory-functions::55.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::55.snippetHtml: Actually, if all we care about is starting with a dice roll and deciding whether the next player moves or not, we can forget coins were ever involved.

series-probability-theory-functions::57.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::57.snippetHtml: Gluing together functions like this is called composition. It always gives another function, called the composite. The source of the composite is the source of the first function, and the target is the target of the second function.

series-probability-theory-functions::58.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::58.snippetHtml: Each arrow in the composite is formed by collapsing a path made from two arrows from the original functions.

series-probability-theory-functions::60.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::60.snippetHtml: The composite doesn't care about what happens in between: the target of the first function, which is the source of the second function, which in this case is the set with $\mathsfheads$ and $\mathsftails$ in it. The composite forgets what happens in between.

series-probability-theory-functions::61.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::61.snippetHtml: Given a function $f\rightarrow Y$ and a function $g\rightarrow Z$, their composite is $g\circ f\rightarrow Z$.

series-probability-theory-functions::62.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::62.snippetHtml: For example, if $f(x_1)=y_1$ and $g(y_1)=z_2$, then $(g\circ f)(x_1)=z_2$. That is:

series-probability-theory-functions::69.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::69.snippetHtml: Since $g\circ f$ is just like applying $f$ and then applying $g$, we can also write $(g\circ f)(x_1)=g(f(x_1))=z_2$, where $f(x_1)$ is the result of $f$ that gets fed to $g$.

series-probability-theory-functions::70.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::70.snippetHtml: This notation might seem weird. We know $g$ is applied after $f$. If we drew one of our diagrams, $g$ would appear on the right (orange arrows). However, in $g\circ f$ it appears on the left! This reversal is related to the notation $g(f(\cdot))$.

series-probability-theory-functions::71.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::71.snippetHtml: To maintain the order seen in our diagrams, we could use the alternate notation $f\compo g: X\rightarrow Z$, where $f\compo g \coloneqq g\circ f$. (The symbol "$\coloneqq$" means "these things are equal by definition, and not as a result of something else".)

series-probability-theory-functions::72.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::72.snippetHtml: In string diagrams, we can simply join functions together as we would in our mapping diagrams.

series-probability-theory-functions::74.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::74.snippetHtml: This is an actual mathematical equation! It says "if we input any $x\in X$ into $f$, then take the output of $f$ and pass it to $g$, then the output of $g$ will be identical to the output of the composite $g\circ f$ if we input the same $x$ into it as we did to $f$".

series-probability-theory-functions::75.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::75.snippetHtml: This particular diagram is a valid way to describe the composition of any function $f\to Y$ with any function $g\to Z$. If we have a specific $f$ and $g$ in mind, we'll have to say so – a string diagram is more abstract, and doesn't show the internal arrows of functions like a mapping diagram would.

series-probability-theory-functions::76.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::76.snippetHtml: Sometimes, we'll omit the wire labels when the context is clear.

series-probability-theory-functions::78.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::78.snippetHtml: We use "$\rightsquigarrow$" in our mapping diagrams to say "we can rewrite this diagram, in this way".

series-probability-theory-functions::79.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::79.snippetHtml: Technically this is different than saying that the two sides of the diagram are equal, like we do when we use "$=$" in a string diagram equation. As mentioned in the preceding box, when two string diagrams are equal that means they represent the same computation.

series-probability-theory-functions::80.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::80.snippetHtml: If this distinction doesn't make sense, don't worry. Just consider that mapping diagrams are a less formal way we can use to write (and re-write) specific examples, while string diagrams are a more formal and general way of describing the computations involved.

series-probability-theory-functions::82.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::82.snippetHtml: There's one more thing we should explore in this post. What does it mean to remember the path you followed—how you arrived where you did?

series-probability-theory-functions::83.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::83.snippetHtml: We've seen that a function doesn't need to reach every point in its target—but some functions do. Our dice rolling function is an example: there was always some way to reach either $\mathsfheads$ or $\mathsftails$.

series-probability-theory-functions::85.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::85.snippetHtml: Functions like this are called "onto"—they map onto the entire target. But notice something else about this function: multiple arrows end in the same place.

series-probability-theory-functions::86.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::86.snippetHtml: A function can have arrows that end in the same place… but some functions don't: each point they reach in their target, they reach only once. These functions are called one-to-one: there's only one point in the source that reaches any one point in the target.

series-probability-theory-functions::87.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::87.snippetHtml: Our mapping from cats and dogs to their diets is an example.

series-probability-theory-functions::89.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::89.snippetHtml: This function is one-to-one, but it isn't onto: nothing reaches $\mathsfherbivores$.

series-probability-theory-functions::90.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::90.snippetHtml: If a function's source is smaller than its target, we know it won't have enough arrows to reach everywhere in the target. It can't be onto. And if a function's target is smaller than its source, then we know it can't be one-to-one—there are more arrows than there are places to go, and some must end in the same place!

series-probability-theory-functions::91.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::91.snippetHtml: If a function $f\rightarrow Y$ is one-to-one, AKA "injective", that means no two arrows can end in the same place. If one arrow starts at $x_1$ and arrives at $f(x_1)$, and another arrow starts at $x_2$ and arrives at $f(x_2)$, then we know that $f(x_1)\neq f(x_2)$.

series-probability-theory-functions::92.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::92.snippetHtml: The rule holds whenever two arrows start at different points in $X$. So $f$ is one-to-one because for every $x_1$ and $x_2$ we could choose from $X$, if $x_1\neq x_2$, then $f(x_1)\neq f(x_2)$.

series-probability-theory-functions::93.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::93.snippetHtml: Similarly, if we know that $f$ is one-to-one and we find out that $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$, then $x_1$ and $x_2$ must actually be the same point in $X$, which for whatever reason we've been referring to by different labels.

series-probability-theory-functions::94.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::94.snippetHtml: If a function $f: X\rightarrow Y$ is onto, AKA "surjective", that means every point in $Y$ must be reached by some arrow in $X$. In other words, for every $y\in Y$, there exists some $x\in X$ for which $f(x) = y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::95.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::95.snippetHtml: A function can be one-to-one, or onto, or both, or neither. We've already seen one that's neither:

series-probability-theory-functions::97.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::97.snippetHtml: We don't reach every point in $\mathsfY$, so we're not onto. And two arrows reach the same point, so we're not one-to-one. But since $\mathsfX$ is the same size as $\mathsfY$, at least it is possible to draw a function that is both one-to-one and onto – called an isomorphism.

series-probability-theory-functions::98.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::98.snippetHtml: There are six possible isomorphisms from $\mathsfX$ to $\mathsfY$.

series-probability-theory-functions::100.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::100.snippetHtml: If our function is an isomorphism, then there's a unique match-up between points in our source and points our target. For each of the six isomorphisms above, it's easy to flip around its arrows to get an inverse function, which goes in the opposite direction.

series-probability-theory-functions::102.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::102.snippetHtml: These inverses are also isomorphisms, and they are the only possible isomorphisms that go "backwards" from $\mathsfY$ to $\mathsfX$. And because they represent unique match-ups, we could of course reverse them again to get the blue ones back.[^8]

series-probability-theory-functions::103.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::103.snippetHtml: Here's a specific example of an isomorphism: a rule that reverses the order of the numbers on our dice. When we roll a 6, we get a 1, and vice versa.

series-probability-theory-functions::105.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::105.snippetHtml: In the last diagram, the set on the right is flipped upside down relative to the one on the left, to make the arrows easier to draw. But the two sets are actually identical. The function and its inverse are reflexive functions: they "reflect" back on the same set they start from.

series-probability-theory-functions::106.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::106.snippetHtml: For a reflexive function, the source and the target are the same, so of course they are the same size. That doesn't mean that all reflexive functions are isomorphisms, though. We could easily make a function that takes every dice roll and converts it into a 6.

series-probability-theory-functions::108.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::108.snippetHtml: This is obviously not one-to-one, and not onto. It's not an isomorphism, and we can't invert it.

series-probability-theory-functions::109.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::109.snippetHtml: If we follow our function, and then its inverse—blue arrow, then orange—we arrive back where we started. We can also follow the inverse first—orange, then blue—and arrive back where we started, on the other side.

series-probability-theory-functions::110.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::110.snippetHtml: In either case, an isomorphism never forgets. And functions that aren't isomorphisms are "forgetful", in a sense. How?

series-probability-theory-functions::111.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::111.snippetHtml: What if my friends and I have the opposite problem we did yesterday? We have a coin, but no dice. Can we just reverse our function from earlier, to get another function that maps coin flips to dice rolls?

series-probability-theory-functions::113.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::113.snippetHtml: We can't. Look at the squiggly arrows – a function can't map $\mathsfheads$ to 1, 2, and 3 all at once. Our function can only have two arrows, but we wanted the possibility of rolling any of the six sides.[^3]

series-probability-theory-functions::114.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::114.snippetHtml: If I tell you that I rolled the dice and the converted result was $\mathsftails$, you have no way of knowing if I actually rolled a 4, 5, or 6. Because the dice-to-coin function isn't one-to-one, some of its arrows end at the same place, and it forgets where it started. Once we follow a blue arrow, we can't follow an orange arrow back, unlike what we could do with the isomorphism.

series-probability-theory-functions::115.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::115.snippetHtml: But just like we could with the isomorphism, we can follow the blue arrows back if we choose some of the orange arrows, and follow them first.

series-probability-theory-functions::117.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::117.snippetHtml: We chose to map $\mathsfheads$ to 2, and $\mathsftails$ to 6. That won't be enough to return us to 1, 3, 4, or 5 (red points) if we follow the blue arrows first. But if we follow the orange arrows first, our blue dice-to-coin function does have the two correct arrows to convert 2 and 6 back to their respective coin flips. So while the blue function does invert the orange one, the opposite is not true.

series-probability-theory-functions::118.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::118.snippetHtml: Actually, the blue dice-to-coin function can invert any such function we choose that converts a coin flip to a dice roll, so long as it reaches 1, 2, or 3 from $\mathsfheads$, and 4, 5, or 6 from $\mathsftails$ – that is, so long as it respects the overall $\mathsfheads$-$\mathsftails$ split of the blue function.

series-probability-theory-functions::120.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::120.snippetHtml: These are all of the possible right inverses of our dice-coin function.

series-probability-theory-functions::121.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::121.snippetHtml: If the blue function is $f\to Y$ and the orange function is $g\to X$, then notice that for all $y\in Y$ (that is, no matter if we start from $\mathsfheads$ or $\mathsftails$) then $f(g(y))=y$, and we arrive back where we started.

series-probability-theory-functions::122.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::122.snippetHtml: However, for some $x\in X$ (specifically 1, 3, 4, and 5), we have $g(f(x))\neq x$.

series-probability-theory-functions::123.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::123.snippetHtml: Notice that in the first case, the one where the inverse actually works, the orange function $g$ is on the right: $f(g(x))$. This is just the same backwards writing that we saw when discussing composition earlier.

series-probability-theory-functions::124.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::124.snippetHtml: There are 9 functions here. We also saw 9 possible functions from a set of size 2 to a set of size 3 earlier.

series-probability-theory-functions::125.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::125.snippetHtml: That's because in both cases, there are only 3 possible places for each arrow to go. Earlier, it was because the target had only 3 points in it. Now, it's because the target is divided into 3 points for heads, and 3 points for tails, which we've colored separately – and each arrow needs to stay on its half of the split.

series-probability-theory-functions::126.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::126.snippetHtml: So that's what happens when a function is onto but not one-to-one. What about the opposite?

series-probability-theory-functions::128.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::128.snippetHtml: We can easily invert the two existing blue arrows, but we have no idea how to return from somewhere we never arrived ($\mathsfherbivores$).[^4]

series-probability-theory-functions::129.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::129.snippetHtml: To invert our function, we have to choose one of the two squiggly arrows to follow.

series-probability-theory-functions::131.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::131.snippetHtml: I mapped $\mathsfherbivores$ to $\mathsfClaire$, since an omnivore is kind of a sometimes-herbivore, I guess. But does that make sense? This is an important reminder that just because the math is flexible and allows you to do something, doesn't mean that it makes sense to do it when you're using the math as a model of something real.

series-probability-theory-functions::132.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::132.snippetHtml: The situation is opposite to what we faced when trying to invert our dice-coin function. If we follow the blue arrows first, the inverse we've chosen can return us to the same starting person, but the extra arrow we had to choose will go unfollowed (grey).

series-probability-theory-functions::133.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::133.snippetHtml: However, if we follow the orange arrows of our inverse first, $\mathsfherbivores$ and $\mathsfomnivores$ both map to Claire and there's no way for us to return to $\mathsfherbivores$ (red).

series-probability-theory-functions::134.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::134.snippetHtml: Here, there are only two possible left inverses: one maps $\mathsfherbivores$ to Claire, like above. The other would map $\mathsfherbivores$ to Max—which seems contradictory with $\mathsfcarnivores$ already mapping to Max, though nothing about the rules of functions alone would stop us from making that choice.

series-probability-theory-functions::135.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::135.snippetHtml: Any function that is one-to-one has at least one left inverse, and any function that is onto has at least one right inverse. If a function is both one-to-one and onto it's an isomorphism, and it has only one inverse, which is both the left and the right inverse—called simply "the" inverse.

series-probability-theory-functions::136.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::136.snippetHtml: If $g\rightarrow Y$ is a one-to-one function with at least one arrow, then there must be a function $h\rightarrow X$ for which $h\comp g = \mathrmid_X$. In other words, if we start in $X$, then follow $g$, then follow $h$, we will arrive back at the same point in $X$ we started from. The composite of the two functions is just $\mathrmid_X$, which takes us from each point in $X$ to the exact same point in $X$. There may be more than one function like $h$ that works this way with $g$, and each one is a left inverse of $g$.

series-probability-theory-functions::137.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::137.snippetHtml: If $p: X\rightarrow Y$ is an onto function with at least one arrow, then there must be a function $q\rightarrow X$ for which $p\comp q = \mathrmid_Y$. So the composite will return us to the identical place in $Y$, if we start from $Y$. Each function like $q$ is called a right inverse of $p$.

series-probability-theory-functions::138.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::138.snippetHtml: If $f\rightarrow Y$ is an isomorphism, then $f^-1: Y \rightarrow X$ is its unique inverse, and we get back to where we started, no matter which side we start on: $f^-1\comp f = \mathrmid_X$ and also $f\comp f^-1 = \mathrmid_Y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::140.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::140.snippetHtml: Next time we'll learn about channels. They're kind of different from the functions we've seen so far, and they'll be the parts we'll build our theory out of.

series-probability-theory-functions::141.title: Functions (Functional Probability)
series-probability-theory-functions::141.snippetHtml: [^3]: Actually, it is possible to use coin flips to simulate dice rolls – but not a single coin flip, which has only two outcomes and can't be mapped to all six sides. [^4]: Why would we want to invert this function? Say Max and Claire are on a team together, and someone mentions "the meat-eater on the team". An inverse function could tell us that they're referring to Max. Of course, if the team were larger, multiple team members' arrows might point to $\mathsfcarnivores$. Then, "the meat-eater" couldn't uniquely refer to Max anymore. [^6]: We've numbered the points because it helps us talk about them. The names don't mean anything else, until we say they do. We aren't saying that $x_1$ is less than $x_2$ just because $1$ comes before $2$, or anything like that. We could just as easily have chosen to name our points $x_1$, $x_\star$, $x_A$, and $y_\odot$, $y_\Omega$, $y_\dagger$ since all we need to do at this time is tell them apart. [^7]: We might also say that our rule expresses a relation that represents a coin using the sides of dice. [^8]: In this case we haven't distinguished the source and target points with labels, so the orange inverses actually appear identical to their respective blue functions, minus the colour change and horizontal mirroring.

series-unclenching-actually::0.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::0.snippetHtml: In my past couple of posts, I’ve made a lot of assumptions and simplifications for the sake of explanation.

series-unclenching-actually::1.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::1.snippetHtml: Now, as if 44 footnotes weren’t enough, let’s expand a bit on some things I haven’t addressed yet, and which I sometimes still find kind of confusing.

series-unclenching-actually::3.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::3.snippetHtml: Suppose a brain can enter a high-energy state, reorganize its activity, and rebalance its influences. Psychologically this should mean the freedom to resettle on better patterns of behaviour.

series-unclenching-actually::4.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::4.snippetHtml: But really, being free to move doesn’t mean I’ll necessarily move to a better place. The context in which I transit a high-energy state is critical:

series-unclenching-actually::5.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::5.snippetHtml:
• If the system is being driven into bad patterns during the annealing process, then those patterns will also have a chance to contract into the influences of the system.
    We could think of PTSD as an annealing event gone wrong: excited by intense and unrelenting inputs, my brain enters a high-energy state and renegotiates its inner contracts under the duress of terror.
    This shouldn’t make us fear annealing in itself, any more than we should fear our capacity for learning more generally. While it’s possible to teach your mind to suffer, with no upside, that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t ever learn again.

series-unclenching-actually::6.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::6.snippetHtml: If the system is being driven into bad patterns during the annealing process, then those patterns will also have a chance to contract into the influences of the system.

series-unclenching-actually::7.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::7.snippetHtml: We could think of PTSD as an annealing event gone wrong: excited by intense and unrelenting inputs, my brain enters a high-energy state and renegotiates its inner contracts under the duress of terror.

series-unclenching-actually::8.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::8.snippetHtml: This shouldn’t make us fear annealing in itself, any more than we should fear our capacity for learning more generally. While it’s possible to teach your mind to suffer, with no upside, that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t ever learn again.

series-unclenching-actually::9.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::9.snippetHtml: • Meditation is nice because it’s semantically neutral with respect to sensory data. But the influences that already exist within the brain are not necessarily neutral with respect to each other! Inducing strong annealing by prolonged meditative practice might end badly if the practitioner does not carefully integrate the sometimes weird and dreamlike consequences that follow when boundaries are softened between flows that had previously been held apart.

series-unclenching-actually::10.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::10.snippetHtml: Meditation is nice because it’s semantically neutral with respect to sensory data. But the influences that already exist within the brain are not necessarily neutral with respect to each other! Inducing strong annealing by prolonged meditative practice might end badly if the practitioner does not carefully integrate the sometimes weird and dreamlike consequences that follow when boundaries are softened between flows that had previously been held apart.

series-unclenching-actually::11.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::11.snippetHtml:
• Drugs, such as psychedelics, may intervene directly in the brain to induce a high-energy state, more or less independently of the sensory data being consumed.
    It does seem pretty useful to have a pharmacological cheat code for annealing. But in the moments after someone takes a drug, it remains to be seen how the learning process will play out, given the sensory data they’re actually consuming. In fact they have to take special care, because they didn’t need to take special care to induce the state in the first place. This is already a meme: set and setting.

series-unclenching-actually::12.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::12.snippetHtml: Drugs, such as psychedelics, may intervene directly in the brain to induce a high-energy state, more or less independently of the sensory data being consumed.

series-unclenching-actually::13.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::13.snippetHtml: It does seem pretty useful to have a pharmacological cheat code for annealing. But in the moments after someone takes a drug, it remains to be seen how the learning process will play out, given the sensory data they’re actually consuming. In fact they have to take special care, because they didn’t need to take special care to induce the state in the first place. This is already a meme: set and setting.

series-unclenching-actually::15.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::15.snippetHtml: Michael Edward Johnson suggests that annealing might be the way we should view learning in the brain. The subtitle of his annealing post is in fact “Toward a Neural Theory of Everything”.

series-unclenching-actually::16.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::16.snippetHtml: Okay… I don’t take this to mean that mechanisms like Hebbian reinforcement (HR) aren’t also “learning in the brain”, but that annealing is part of a larger account of how such lower-level mechanisms are coordinated, up to the behavioural level. I agree with Johnson (and others) that a central, unresolved problem of neuroscience is to bridge the neural and behavioural levels. It makes limited sense to ask how a synapse is changing, without asking what the organism it belongs to is doing.

series-unclenching-actually::18.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::18.snippetHtml: I’ve played a bit fast and loose with thermodynamics. This series wasn’t meant to be formal, but I think I should give a little more, here.

series-unclenching-actually::19.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::19.snippetHtml: Classic equations for free energy have a form like:

series-unclenching-actually::20.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::20.snippetHtml: Here, U is the internal energy. The more energy is bound up in the structure of the system, the higher U is. A really hardened piece of steel with lots of little stresses has a relatively high value of U. There’s a lot of energy trapped in such a system; certain processes can potentially relieve the stresses and release that energy. So we might also call U the potentialenergy.

series-unclenching-actually::21.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::21.snippetHtml: The interpretation is similar for brains. Higher U can mean more complex models, which are necessary and good because the world is complex. But it also means more unnecessary complexity, structural mess, or technical debt. That’s bad, when it interferes with the movement and harmony of the system.

series-unclenching-actually::22.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::22.snippetHtml: Thermodynamics is about taking a bird’s-eye view: instead of keeping track of all the little details, we keep track of summary values like U, the total internal energy. The temperature T is another such value, summarizing how much kinetic energy all the system’s parts have — how much they’re moving around.

series-unclenching-actually::23.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::23.snippetHtml: S is the entropy. It measures our uncertainty about the detailed state of the system, given that we’re working with summaries. If there are lots of ways that we could subtly rearrange the system without changing what the summary says, then the summary can’t tell us which of those subtle differences actually describes the system at the moment. So S is high.

series-unclenching-actually::24.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::24.snippetHtml: Our equation describes how U, S, and T combine to give free energy F. But free energy isn’t really meaningful on its own unless we’re considering some process (like annealing) that changes S and/or U. So we write instead:

series-unclenching-actually::25.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::25.snippetHtml: Here, ΔU and ΔS are the changes in the values of U and S, due to the process.[^1]

series-unclenching-actually::26.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::26.snippetHtml: Processes that are “allowed” to happen, that are spontaneous or favourable, have negative ΔF. This implies negative ΔU and/or positive ΔS: processes that release bound energy are favourable, as are processes that increase the entropy. Sometimes the two can be at odds with each other (e.g. negative ΔU and negative ΔS); changing the temperature T is one way to alter this balance.

series-unclenching-actually::27.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::27.snippetHtml: The relaxation of stresses due to heating should have negative, favourable ΔU. But is the ΔS of destressing positive or negative? Watching explanations on YouTube and skimming materials science papers has left me confused. On the one hand, it seems intuitively correct that destressing decreases entropy: a more regular lattice is more correlated with itself. But maybe this is misleading, an overly static snapshot. Atoms are always moving, and if the atoms in a regular lattice are more free to shift around (i.e. their potential basins are wider) than tangled atoms are at the same temperature, then perhaps the regular lattice is higher entropy?

series-unclenching-actually::28.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::28.snippetHtml: In any case, imagine that the ΔF of a process like destressing is technically favourable at a lower temperature, but in practice we still need to heat the system to actually see something happen. Why would that be?

series-unclenching-actually::29.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::29.snippetHtml: Well, a process can be favourable, but that doesn’t mean it happens quickly enough to matter. The free energy equation is a summary of everything that happens between the endpoints of a process, and doesn’t account for the detailed dynamics of the subprocesses by which things actually play out in between. If we look at the ΔF between two room-temperature pieces of metal in different states, it might seem that one should just spontaneously change to be more like the other. But that won’t happen until we provide enough energy to activate the intermediate processes. The rate at which those processes happen typically accelerates rapidly as temperature increases.

series-unclenching-actually::30.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::30.snippetHtml: Now, the free energy principle is concerned with a problem of information: how to infer which hypotheses H are the best explanations of some data D. In those terms, this is how it defines the free energy:

series-unclenching-actually::31.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::31.snippetHtml: This looks complicated, but it’s analogous to the equations we’ve already seen.[^2] The two terms (“𝔼…” and “H…”) still correspond to energy and entropy[^3], and they still describe something like the internal complexity of our model, versus how uncertain we are about the state of the world.[^4]

series-unclenching-actually::32.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::32.snippetHtml: Needless to say I’m not exactly sure how all of this applies to annealing in metallurgy, let alone to the brain. (I’m not the only one.) But importantly, the free energy principle is a principle. It’s a statistical summary of what the system’s information will be doing overall, and not a claim about the details of the system’s implementation.

series-unclenching-actually::34.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::34.snippetHtml: I’m a little confused about the balance between coherence and incoherence, and what exactly constitutes a high-energy state for the brain.

series-unclenching-actually::35.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::35.snippetHtml: This paper suggests that the brain at baseline is already slightly above criticality, and that LSD significantly increases the disorder of the system:

series-unclenching-actually::36.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::36.snippetHtml: However, at least in our model and as already described in previous work using similar methods [5, 6], we found that the resting brain in the placebo condition was already above the critical point—that is, the resting, the wakeful brain is in a supercritical state as observed through the Ising framework lens. This is consistent with the idea that, while mutual information peaks at the critical temperature, information flow in such systems peaks in the disordered (paramagnetic) phase [98], which is in apparent contradiction with other studies suggesting a subcritical nature of healthy brain dynamics [39].

series-unclenching-actually::37.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::37.snippetHtml: However, at least in our model and as already described in previous work using similar methods [5, 6], we found that the resting brain in the placebo condition was already above the critical point—that is, the resting, the wakeful brain is in a supercritical state as observed through the Ising framework lens. This is consistent with the idea that, while mutual information peaks at the critical temperature, information flow in such systems peaks in the disordered (paramagnetic) phase [98], which is in apparent contradiction with other studies suggesting a subcritical nature of healthy brain dynamics [39].

series-unclenching-actually::38.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::38.snippetHtml: And apparently there isn’t a single, invariant way to define criticality anyway:

series-unclenching-actually::39.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::39.snippetHtml: Diverse and inconsistent uses of the terms “critical” and “criticality” have led to confusion. In this review, criticality has mostly referred to avalanche dynamics that behave at the limit between stability and instability. But other variants of criticality exist (Wilting and Priesemann, 2019). These include criticality between ordered and chaotic phases called the “edge of chaos” (Boedecker et al., 2012), criticality between synchrony and asynchrony (Botcharova et al., 2014), and multiple paradigms for the time-evolution of a critical phase transition as in extended criticality, intermittent criticality, and self-organized criticality (Saleur et al., 1996; Huang et al., 1998; Sammis and Smith, 1999; Bowman and Sammis, 2004). These forms of dynamical criticality are also distinct from statistical criticality (Mora and Bialek, 2011; Tkačik et al., 2013). How these all inter-connect is a topic of ongoing research.

series-unclenching-actually::40.snippetHtml: Diverse and inconsistent uses of the terms “critical” and “criticality” have led to confusion. series-unclenching-actually::41.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::41.snippetHtml: Say we want to study multi-scale learning processes like annealing. How should we define and measure brain criticality, or high-energy states? Will the answer vary across the brain, the behaviour, the experiment? How will we notice when we are lumping too much stuff together in our summaries, relative to the causality we should want to describe?

series-unclenching-actually::43.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::43.snippetHtml: I wouldn’t blame you for imagining totally distinct phases of relaxation and contraction in the brain, given my simplified description of annealing. But is it plausible that the mechanisms that reinforce versus rebalance the influences between neurons are engaged exclusively, one at a time?

series-unclenching-actually::44.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::44.snippetHtml: Pure HR causes instability in networks because of runaway positive feedback between synaptic weights and firing activities. Normally though, it doesn’t cause instability in the brain. Something must be balancing things out; some other mechanism must be active around the same time. Homeostatic plasticity was one candidate for such a balancing mechanism, but it turned out to be much too slow to keep up with HR. Some other mechanisms, like heterosynaptic plasticity, are faster and might serve a similar role. But it remains to be seen exactly how the balance is maintained, and how much it depends on the detailed structure of individual cells (which varies quite a bit across the brain).

series-unclenching-actually::45.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::45.snippetHtml: Anyway, we should probably not assume that 1) rebalancing does not happen outside of high-energy states, and 2) that HR cannot be active when the system is moving through such states. In fact, interventions that are intended to induce rebalancing might instead be “hijacked” by excessive HR and lead to further entrenchment of harmful behaviour.

series-unclenching-actually::46.title: Actually... (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-actually::46.snippetHtml:
we speculate that there at least two ways in which stress may contribute to canalization in brain circuits and synaptic connections, one would entail chronic stress-induced cortical atrophy (Dias-Ferreira et al., 2009; Duman and Duman, 2015) and another would entail a Hebbian ‘hijacking’ of stress-induced increases in TEMP (Brivio et al., 2020), see also (Parr et al., 2020; Friston et al., 2012b, 2021) – and (Dias-Ferreira et al., 2009; Moda-Sava et al., 2019).
