series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::73.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::73.snippetHtml: • Intelligence is a universal solvent, capable of inventing contexts in which tigers are truly irrelevant as threats. When was the last time you had to stab something? But intelligence is a relative latecomer: hiding and running and stabbing were the intellectual peak of threat-handling for hundreds of millions of years. That was the relentless context in which evolution laid the foundations of our brain’s architecture. And evolution cannot backtrack on its creations, only elaborate on them, however exquisite those elaborations may be.[^19]

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::75.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::75.snippetHtml: So we’re prone to a low-level clenchiness, a flinchy short-sightedness which can corrupt our intelligence. On the other hand, given the chance, we can moderate clenchiness by making wise decisions like “I should probably anneal a bit more than the heirloom inductive biases I got at Tiger World have led me to expect”. Our goals and skills are more complex than ever, and more in need of careful and repeated revision. How do you know you’re doing as well as you could? Evolution is merciless. Self-deception is easy. If there are tigers in this city, they are in a zoo.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::76.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::76.snippetHtml: Corruption or no, I shouldn’t be surprised when most of the time, my adult brain wields its powers of suppression to keep itself in a relatively low-energy state, where it can coordinate more robustly by leaning into the patterns it already knows, while suppressing “irrelevant” details.[^20] Over time though, circumstances may build and build to the realization that things could improve, and that progress isn’t being made by incrementally adjusting the individual parts while otherwise maintaining the status quo. Then it’s probably time to risk a temporary hit to robustness and experience a whole-brain annealing event: let the parts disintegrate and reform!

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::77.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::77.snippetHtml: Michael Edward Johnson has been writing about annealing and brains for a while, and he’s made some deeper connections than I’ll make with this post.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::78.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::78.snippetHtml: One thing I want to highlight is his discussion of Selen Atasoy’s studies of brain harmonics. It’s new to me, but I’ll make a first pass connecting Atasoy’s work to what we’ve already discussed.[^21]

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::79.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::79.snippetHtml: First, here’s a new analogy: when we fix a guitar string at both ends and tension it, it tends to oscillate at certain natural frequencies, also called harmonics. This is because when each point on the string moves up and down, it influences each of its neighbouring points on the string to do the same. As long as they remain physically connected, neighbouring points must move together and oscillate at similar frequencies. The overall result is that when the string is excited, the entire thing “locks on” to a particular resonant state or mode where the entire string oscillates as a whole. The frequencies at which this happens are determined by the influences physically holding the string together, and their geometry. In the case of a guitar string, that includes the material properties of steel or nylon, the thickness and length of the string between the tensioning points, and the tension the string is under (i.e. how much we turn the tuning peg).

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::81.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::81.snippetHtml: An oscillating string, held under tension between two points (black). The first four harmonics are shown. Higher harmonics have higher frequencies—they oscillate more quickly—and they subdivide the string with more nodes (red) at which the string happens to be stationary, but isn’t fixed. Note that this figure does not show the effect of material, thickness, tension, or (actual) length, all of which would change the real frequencies that these harmonics would correspond to, if this were a real string. (Source.)

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::82.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::82.snippetHtml: Again, a brain is more complex than this — but let’s speculate. Imagine a brain as a kind of complex resonator. Which modes will it resonate at? That depends on the influences between its parts, which we can also frame as the connectivity of the paths along which neural activity travels and loops and reverberates.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::83.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::83.snippetHtml: Harmonics may arise within a brain region due to the local influences, but also across the whole brain due to the larger-scale influences across all its regions, sometimes called the connectome. Atasoy’s theory is called Connectome-Specific Harmonic Waves (CSHWs); it’s a way to predict the large-scale resonant harmonics of the brain based on MRI measurements of the connectome’s structure:

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::84.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::84.snippetHtml:
[CSHW is] a method for applying harmonic analysis to the brain: basically, it uses various forms of brain imaging to infer what the brain’s natural resonant frequencies (eigenmodes) are, and how much energy each of these frequencies have. The core workflow is three steps: first combine MRI and DTI to approximate a brain’s connectome, then with an empirically-derived wave propagation equation calculate what the natural harmonics are of this connectome, then estimate which power distribution between these harmonics would most accurately reconstruct the observed fMRI activity.

  • Michael Edward Johnson

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::85.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::85.snippetHtml: [CSHW is] a method for applying harmonic analysis to the brain: basically, it uses various forms of brain imaging to infer what the brain’s natural resonant frequencies (eigenmodes) are, and how much energy each of these frequencies have. The core workflow is three steps: first combine MRI and DTI to approximate a brain’s connectome, then with an empirically-derived wave propagation equation calculate what the natural harmonics are of this connectome, then estimate which power distribution between these harmonics would most accurately reconstruct the observed fMRI activity.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::88.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::88.snippetHtml: Johnson [proposed](https://opentheory.net/2019/11/neural-annealing-toward-a-neural-theory-of-everything/#:~=a continuum of CSHWs) a continuum of harmonics, across scales of the brain. Smaller-scale harmonics — which he categorized as region-specific harmonic waves (RSHWs) — should have higher frequencies, be confined to local regions, and correspond to (sub-)behavioural particulars. Larger-scale harmonics (Atasoy’s CSHWs) should have lower frequencies, pass through many regions, and reflect behavioural coordination or summary states.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::89.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::89.snippetHtml: I find “CSHWs” and “RSHWs” a little disorienting to look at, so for the rest of this post I’m going to say LHs for little/local harmonics and BHs for big/brain harmonics.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::90.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::90.snippetHtml: LHs are high-frequency harmonics that are confined to local brain regions which deal in particulars. It makes sense that they are confined; we should expect different particulars not to interfere with each other by crossing their local boundaries, otherwise our brains might have trouble keeping track of particulars. (It does strike me as redundant to say that LHs are locally confined when we’ve already said that they are high-frequency, since the geometry of confinement is precisely what determines the frequency of resonance. I’m probably missing something.)

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::91.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::91.snippetHtml: How can all these isolated LH particulars be coordinated into coherent behaviour? That should happen at the scale of the BHs, which being lower frequency have a more coherent identity across the whole brain. They travel widely, and should be able to interact with the many local LHs. And that goes both ways. For example:

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::92.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::92.snippetHtml: • LHs to BHs: If the right LHs start resonating differently after being struck by some new and surprising details, their voices might be able to resynchronize the BHs and produce an overall shift in emotions or behaviour.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::93.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::93.snippetHtml: LHs to BHs: If the right LHs start resonating differently after being struck by some new and surprising details, their voices might be able to resynchronize the BHs and produce an overall shift in emotions or behaviour.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::94.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::94.snippetHtml: • BHs to LHs: An especially loud BH may be able to forcefully synchronize all the LHs and quickly suppress “irrelevant” details.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::95.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::95.snippetHtml: BHs to LHs: An especially loud BH may be able to forcefully synchronize all the LHs and quickly suppress “irrelevant” details.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::96.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::96.snippetHtml: Johnson associates BHs with emotional states. This seems natural, if we treat emotions as a kind of high-level judgment the brain makes about everything it’s doing at the moment. We should expect such judgments to integrate many details from across the brain, and also to influence the processes that deal in those details. BHs are one plausible way in which this could happen.[^22]

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::97.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::97.snippetHtml: This framing is kind of nice, because “the brain maintains a status quo by suppressing apparent irrelevancies” can be bridged to something a little more intuitive or psychological: a game of “good vibes only” is always playing out in the synchronizations and suppressions of harmonics:

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::98.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::98.snippetHtml:
we doctor our [harmonic modes] all the time—when a nice sensation enters our awareness, we reflexively try to ‘grab’ it and stabilize the resonance; when something unpleasant comes in, we try to push away and deaden the resonance

  • Michael Edward Johnson

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::99.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::99.snippetHtml: we doctor our [harmonic modes] all the time—when a nice sensation enters our awareness, we reflexively try to ‘grab’ it and stabilize the resonance; when something unpleasant comes in, we try to push away and deaden the resonance

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::102.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::102.snippetHtml: Johnson makes an interesting [connection](https://opentheory.net/2019/11/neural-annealing-toward-a-neural-theory-of-everything/#:~=Toward a generalized definition of trauma) to trauma and depression. In the event that some LHs become seriously miscalibrated with respect to the particulars they intend to model, it may make sense to turn down the BHs so that miscalibration (misinformation?) cannot spread across the brain like a harmonic infection and cause a “cascading system failure”. The result? The now-quieter BHs aren’t enough to coordinate the LHs, which fall more and more strongly into their own distinct routines, and in a vicious circle this makes it more difficult for a stronger BH to arise again and coordinate them. (Sound familiar?) And so sometimes the outcome is a muted cacophony of unreconciled horrors, bound by history, full of little tensions set at odds with one other.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::103.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::103.snippetHtml: Brain-wide annealing can be framed as relaxing and energizing the harmonics, so that the whole system can reharmonize. It’s like introducing Whoopi Goldberg to a bunch of nuns. And given that the brain is usually trying to maintain a status quo, we might expect annealing to happen locally to the LHs before it happens globally to the BHs.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::104.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::104.snippetHtml:
Insofar as partitioning is possible in a broadly-coupled harmonic system, these [free-energy increasing] perturbations [that would induce annealing] will tend to be ‘local’ as the brain has strong incentives to preserve structure that doesn’t need updating.

  • Michael Edward Johnson

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::105.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::105.snippetHtml: Insofar as partitioning is possible in a broadly-coupled harmonic system, these [free-energy increasing] perturbations [that would induce annealing] will tend to be ‘local’ as the brain has strong incentives to preserve structure that doesn’t need updating.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::108.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::108.snippetHtml: And what are the actual things I can do, to make this happen?

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::109.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::109.snippetHtml: Finally, let’s review a few methods we might expect to induce annealing. (We might also call them treatments to relieve clenching.) Keep in mind that these aren’t recommendations — the circumstances of your own life will determine the best course, of course.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::110.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::110.snippetHtml: I’ve largely based this section on insights I’ve obtained, again, from Michael Edward Johnson. Before we begin, I want to refresh by sharing his convenient summary of the neural annealing process.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::111.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::111.snippetHtml:
1. First, energy (neural excitation, e.g. Free Energy from prediction errors) builds up in the brain, either gradually or suddenly, collecting disproportionately in the brain’s natural eigenmodes [i.e. resonant harmonics];
  2. This build-up of energy (rate of neural firing) crosses a metastability threshold and the brain enters a high-energy state, causing entropic disintegration (weakening previously ‘sticky’ attractors);
  3. The brain’s neurons self-organize into new multi-scale equilibria (attractors), aka implicit assumptions about reality’s structure and value weightings, which given present information should generate lower levels of prediction error than previous models (this is implicitly both a resynchronization of internal predictive models with the environment, and a minimization of dissonance in connectome-specific harmonic waves);
  4. The brain ‘cools’ (neural activity levels slowly return to normal), and parts of the new self-organized patterns remain and become part of the brain’s normal activity landscape;
  5. The cycle repeats, as the brain’s models become outdated and prediction errors start to build up again.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::122.snippetHtml: Here, “self-organize into new multi-scale equilibria” refers to the fancy things that happen near criticality, the sweet spot between cold coherence and hot incoherence.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::123.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::123.snippetHtml: In particular, leading from step 3 into step 4 is where we expect mechanisms such as heterosynaptic plasticity to be activated so that new patterns can be reinforced in the influences within the network, to remain accessible outside of high-energy states.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::136.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::136.snippetHtml: How do we initiate this cascade from step 1?

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::138.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::138.snippetHtml: Earlier in the series we discussed some meditative practices. Now our hypothesis is simple: when applied effectively, meditation pumps excitatory energy into the brain’s networks, potentially inducing high-energy states and reorganization events.[^23]

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::139.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::139.snippetHtml: Excitatory energy? This might seem to contradict the popular view of meditation as tranquil or something. But consider what it means, here: to excite our brain networks, we either need to stop our top-down predictive models from suppressing incoming sensory signals, or we need to boost the intensity of those signals. Or both. This rather lines up with the distinction between insight and concentration practices:

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::140.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::140.snippetHtml: • Insight practices, such as mindfulness, sort of look like removing the habitual top-down suppression (or “judgment”) of “irrelevant” perceptions, allowing them to rise up freely. This should increase the variety (i.e. entropy) of the states we end up reaching.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::141.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::141.snippetHtml: Insight practices, such as mindfulness, sort of look like removing the habitual top-down suppression (or “judgment”) of “irrelevant” perceptions, allowing them to rise up freely. This should increase the variety (i.e. entropy) of the states we end up reaching.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::142.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::142.snippetHtml: • Concentration practices look like focusing all our attention on a single point of perception, greatly boosting its signal.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::143.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::143.snippetHtml: Concentration practices look like focusing all our attention on a single point of perception, greatly boosting its signal.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::144.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::144.snippetHtml: Outside of meditative practice, it’s totally possible for your brain to arrive in a high-energy state because of large, surprising signals related to your children, or your job, or an illness. High-energy states induced in such ways are like loaded questions: they do induce freedom of reorganization… but the system is forced to reform around something specific. Existing influences relax, only to forcibly contract on whatever meaningful and inevitable pattern is being driven into the network at that time. Sometime it’s a pattern we want, or will be happy we found, which is great. But sometimes we’d prefer to clean up the mess we already have, before taking on some more.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::145.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::145.snippetHtml: What’s special about meditation is that it isn’t necessarily about anything. Insight practice often avoids privileging any particular thought. And while concentration practice might seem to privilege some object of attention or other (e.g. the breath), consider that the end result of focusing attention to a truly single point is the collapse of all informative contrasts and associations. Because of this, we should expect these meditative practices to be very useful for cleaning up messes without forcing them to be replaced with something else.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::146.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::146.snippetHtml: Johnson has a term for practices that pump in “content-free” energy: semantically-neutral annealing.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::147.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::147.snippetHtml:
“Semantically neutral energy” refers to neural activity which is not strongly associated with any specific cognitive or emotional process. […] usually energy build-up is limited: once a perturbation of the system neatly falls into a pattern recognized by the brain’s predictive hierarchy, the neural activity propagating this pattern is dissipated.

[…] effortful attention on excitatory bottom-up sense-data and attenuation of inhibitory top-down predictive models will naturally lead to a build-up of this ‘non-semantic’ energy in the brain

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::151.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::151.snippetHtml: Why are serotonergic psychedelics increasingly studied for the treatment of mental illness? Because they might be effective. Why should they be effective? The hypothesis is, again, that they can drive the brain into a high-energy state.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::152.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::152.snippetHtml: Meditation adds energy to the system by changing how we actively reflect, attend, and (dis)inhibit our mental processes, which are either identical or interdependent with our brain states (thus influence them). On the other hand, if psychedelics add energy it’s by directly intervening in the mechanisms of the brain: by turning a kind of chemical tuning knob, they cause some types of neurons to be more easily excited, so that you’ll go high-energy no matter your prior mental state. And the rebalancing mechanisms presumably still get activated — a high-energy state is a high-energy state, to a short-sighted neuron.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::157.snippetHtml: When viewed through a lens of simulated annealing, other neuronal phenomena such as increased: asynchronous glutamate release (Aghajanian and Marek, 1999), expression of neural activity markers (Gresch et al., 2002), complexity of spontaneous oscillatory activity (Schartner et al., 2017), entropy of connectivity motifs (Tagliazucchi et al., 2014), high-frequency harmonics (Atasoy et al., 2017), near (Toker et al., 2022), or supercritical dynamics (Ruffini et al., 2022) sensitivity to perturbation (Jobst et al., 2021), and global integration (Tagliazucchi et al., 2016) can all be linked to either an early, upstream temperature or entropy increase (Schartner et al., 2017) or a later, downstream synaptic reweighting effect e.g., as implied by preclinical data (Shao et al., 2021; Daws et al., 2022; Moda-Sava et al., 2019; Raval et al., 2021).

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::161.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::161.snippetHtml: Two of the canalization authors (Carhart-Harris and Friston) published the REBUS model[^24] of psychedelics in 2019, which — along with adopting the annealing analogy — explained the action of psychedelics in terms of a reduction in precision-weighting on priors, which means the same thing as flattening the energy landscape.[^25] With respect to psychedelics, the main contribution of the canal paper was to give the REBUS model a more dynamical (and perhaps more intuitive) frame — in terms of shallower channels in an energy landscape, rather than decreased pointiness of prior distributions.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::163.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::163.snippetHtml: There seems to be plenty of evidence that exercise is good for mental illness. It could lead to rebalancing in at least a couple of ways:

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::164.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::164.snippetHtml:
• Rhythmic or textural changes in perception can be exciting, but are often relatively semantically neutral.[^26] For example, running on uneven ground creates rhythmic variations which are not very relevant to higher-order predictions, but should not be entirely suppressed.
    As we move through a changing and unfamiliar environment, our sensory fields are filled with shifting textures and motions. As I begin my run, maybe my brain is wearing an inhibitory mask that filters out many of the details; but after an hour or two of attrition, the neutral energy might start to creep in.

    Let’s walk, or bike, or hike a while away

    until the world, long pouring through our eyes

    unfills our minds — and as recedes the day,

    our joy flows in much fuller; much more sound

    our words ignite; our dreams grow more profound —

    and with the sun but brighter will we rise.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::177.snippetHtml: There you have it: hot atoms, cool lattices, rebalancing acts, upward-downward negotiations, suppression signals, brain resonances, and clenching treatments. Quite enough for one post, no?

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::182.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::182.snippetHtml: Also, if you’re wondering “doesn’t entropy always increase?”: the brain is not a closed system. My body spends chemical energy and increases the overall entropy of the universe, so it can reduce its internal entropy.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::184.snippetHtml: [^4]: A metallic crystal is different from a crystal of (say) quartz, or ice. When metal atoms bond, their outermost electrons remain free to interact or shift. This is why metals can be 1) such good conductors, and 2) malleable and ductile.

Even though by heating the metal I did cause its atoms to escape their prior, relatively static disorder, the hot states they enter are dynamically disordered. Suddenly cooling the system traps the atoms in whatever state they happen to be in at the moment, without letting them settle into their preferred equilibrium.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::193.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::193.snippetHtml: Along a hierarchy, it’s appealing to expect progressively “higher” layers to deal with progressively more abstract predictions. The “low” layers of my ventral visual stream tend to be excited by unexpected edges or lines in images; the “higher” layers, by unexpected shapes or objects. Predictive coding suggests that when the object-layer has already concluded that a bird is flying leftward across my field of view, it will send down predictions to the edges-layer: a bunch of bird-forming edges should be appearing lefter-and-lefter. So when the bird moves suddenly rightward, this creates prediction errors in the edges-layer which are sent up to the object-layer — which changes its mind about where the “entire bird” is really heading.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::194.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::194.snippetHtml: Of course, we don’t actually predict everything that falls on our retinas, and most edges and shapes are actually unexpected.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::200.snippetHtml: [^16]: If I can access many different patterns (including the desirable ones) when I’m in a high-energy state, why shouldn’t I stay in that state all the time? Because there is a tradeoff between being able to access any pattern (high entropy) and being able to produce a given pattern robustly (low entropy). More on that in just a moment.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::201.snippetHtml: [^17]: Why should we expect this? Take the perspective of reinforcement learning and evolution:

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::202.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::202.snippetHtml: When the usual associations we’d make are missing, that’s when exploration is most adaptive. When our environment is unfamiliar — when we can’t get away with doctoring our perceptions to insist that it is familiar — that’s when we have the most to gain from relaxing our prior vibes or beliefs, and re-balancing the dynamics of our neural networks.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::203.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::203.snippetHtml: Being in an unfamiliar environment increases the entropy in our brains — it introduces a bunch of variation in our perceptions that’s more difficult to explain away. So shouldn’t the brain’s parts respond to the local signs of increased entropy by re-balancing themselves? And what would happen if evolution had not harnessed mechanisms that allowed this to happen?

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::204.snippetHtml: [^18]: This is directly related to both the plasticity-stability dilemma of neural networks, and the explore-exploit tradeoff of reinforcement learning.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::205.snippetHtml: [^19]: This is a kind of steelman of the “reptile brain” nonsense. No, your brain is not an onion with a tiny reptile inside. No, new structures aren’t simply tacked on top of old ones. But the dynamical topology of evolved systems cannot be simply overwritten or backtracked by further evolution.

series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::206.title: Iron: Your brain (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-iron-your-brain::206.snippetHtml: It is possible to learn efficiency, fluency, and mastery. It is possible to confidently relax in the face of threats. But to achieve these things without the benefit of some discrete high-energy annealing events, if that’s even possible, requires that we find ourselves flowing down just the right learning trajectory. Who’s to say most of us should be so lucky, in the landscape our society already provides?

series-unclenching-practice::1.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::1.snippetHtml: After reading the paper on robust reaching, I began to use "clenching" as a metaphor: not only to speak of lingering tensions of the muscles, but also tensions of the mind—when I lean in and fake it a little too long and hard. And also to refer to situations where, looking in from the outside, a person or a group appears to be trapped[^1]: doubling down, neglecting what might free them, often scarcely even able to look for it.

series-unclenching-practice::2.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::2.snippetHtml: So, how can we unclench? How can we see from the outside?

series-unclenching-practice::3.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::3.snippetHtml: Most of us are falling in most of the time. We wake up and we’re immediately pulled onto the tracks, onto a train of feelings for the people and things around us. Our eyelids lift, our ears alert, and we’re carried forward by sensations, one after another, on automatic. Feelings, into motions, into sensations, into feelings—I want, so I move, so I see, so I want, so…

series-unclenching-practice::4.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::4.snippetHtml: We go back to sleep filled with expectation—an inertia, more or less subliminal—for the next episode[^2].

series-unclenching-practice::5.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::5.snippetHtml: It’s easy to forget that comfort is not a literal property of a lover, nor satisfaction a property of chocolate, nor pleasure a property of porn. Comfort, satisfaction, and pleasure are feelings we have. They happen inside our heads, where our subjectivity actually lives, where a simulation of the world blazes along, fed by our senses. We easily confuse the simulation with the outside world it simulates—the map with the territory. Because it’s convenient. Because it would be a disorienting burden on our limited attention, to be always and viscerally reminded that we don’t experience the rest of the world directly. Instead, evolution has seen that it’s robust for us to lean right in to whichever simplifications bring us those feelings. As much as we can get away with it, anyway. So we keep falling, keep pushing buttons, keep forgetting they’re buttons. And before long this fails, inevitably, and leaves us shaken and disappointed.[^3] The world is always one step beyond button-mashing story-logic. My lover is a real person. Chocolate isn’t a balanced diet. Porn isn’t living sex.

series-unclenching-practice::6.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::6.snippetHtml: How can you become wise to these property illusions? How can you see from the outside? By practicing not falling in, like any other skill. By taking regular time to intentionally redirect attention back upon itself: to learn what it really means to give attention, and to stop giving attention. To make room, and witness as it fills with something new.

series-unclenching-practice::7.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::7.snippetHtml: With practice, we can learn to change how attention and feelings move, for the better.[^4]

series-unclenching-practice::8.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::8.snippetHtml: I can still keep the patterns I want to keep—still feel comfort from people, and satisfaction from food. Of course I don’t want to abandon everything, to jettison all meaning and enjoyment and success. I want to notice a little sooner when willing attachment starts to turn to willful captivity. To see beyond the familiar playground-prison of my room, my home, my neighbourhood, my school, my workplace… To learn what other movements could be possible.[^5] To be ready to act (or not) at the first spark of evidence or opportunity. To be empowered, and walk in a wider world. And to find out just how deeply and smoothly and vastly my feelings can work.

series-unclenching-practice::9.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::9.snippetHtml: What is meditation? Maybe, the practice of not just falling in. But the meditative practices that people actually follow are much more varied and messy than that little summary suggests.

series-unclenching-practice::10.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::10.snippetHtml: Buddhists and meditation nerds seem to refer to pretty much any intentional activity that’s relevant to personal or spiritual development as practice. I want to take some time to share my current thoughts about practice, and how they could relate to the other things we’ve discussed in this series.[^6]

series-unclenching-practice::12.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::12.snippetHtml: 1. Concentration practices are about intensifying certain states of mind, and unifying attention. These states include metta, or feelings of benevolence towards others, as emphasized by “loving-kindness meditation”. They also include absorption in the jhānas, which are states of detached bliss—mental euphoria, bodily pleasure, and ultimately equanimity—that can be reached when we are freed or isolated enough from familiar objects, and the distractions of falling-in. On the surface the jhānas might seem kind of dangerous. We’ll return to that that shortly.

series-unclenching-practice::14.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::14.snippetHtml: 1. Insight practices are about picking apart states of your mind—contemplating aspects of them, and witnessing patterns and conflicts. An example is vipassanā, which is based in the contemplation of the fleeting nature of experience.

series-unclenching-practice::15.snippetHtml: Insight practices are about picking apart states of your mind—contemplating aspects of them, and witnessing patterns and conflicts. An example is vipassanā, which is based in the contemplation of the fleeting nature of experience.

series-unclenching-practice::16.snippetHtml: 1. Integration practices are about relating and connecting your insights to your entire life. Many of these practices don’t look like “meditation”. For example: seeing therapists, having conversations, writing online, changing habits (including meditation practices)…

series-unclenching-practice::17.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::17.snippetHtml: Integration practices are about relating and connecting your insights to your entire life. Many of these practices don’t look like “meditation”. For example: seeing therapists, having conversations, writing online, changing habits (including meditation practices)…

series-unclenching-practice::18.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::18.snippetHtml: The three kinds of practice are mutually strengthening:

series-unclenching-practice::19.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::19.snippetHtml: 1. Better concentration creates the conditions for insight. Mindfulness practitioners emphasize concentrating on the present moment to enable a clear, non-judgmental awareness of mental events. In vipassanā, concentrating on the breath is a basis for insight into the transitory. And the concentrated positive vibes of metta and the jhanas are powerful vantages from which to contemplate goodness, love, and happiness, from above the clouds of petty inclinations and grievances.

We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful what we pretend to be.

- Kurt Vonnegut

series-unclenching-practice::27.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::27.snippetHtml: We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful what we pretend to be.

series-unclenching-practice::29.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::29.snippetHtml: Like pretty much everything, meditation is not completely safe. Some practitioners claim emphatically that it’s dangerous, at least once you’ve reached the scale of hundreds or thousands of hours of practice.

series-unclenching-practice::30.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::30.snippetHtml: As we grow and learn across our lives, our minds build up structure. Our mental movements come to weave among each other like so many threads. As Mark Lippmann[^7] has pointed out, this process of accumulation of structure is like the concept of technical debt in software engineering, “the implied cost of future reworking required when choosing an easy but limited solution instead of a better approach that could take more time”:

series-unclenching-practice::31.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::31.snippetHtml: When a mind is really surprised, or things are happening too fast, or something is just too hard, or a mind enacts ingrained bad habits, in all these cases a mind takes on technical debt in order to keep dealing with the world in real time. The more technical debt a mind has, the harder it is for that mind to solve problems moving forward, so technical debt begets more technical debt.

series-unclenching-practice::32.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::32.snippetHtml: When a mind is really surprised, or things are happening too fast, or something is just too hard, or a mind enacts ingrained bad habits, in all these cases a mind takes on technical debt in order to keep dealing with the world in real time. The more technical debt a mind has, the harder it is for that mind to solve problems moving forward, so technical debt begets more technical debt.

series-unclenching-practice::33.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::33.snippetHtml: To put this in terms we’ve already used: when we cannot predict what will happen, when we have no time to try out new models or respond precisely to disturbances, we find simplifications to lean into. We fake it ‘til we make it. But our fakery will inevitably be inappropriate to our changing situation—like pulling on a finger trap isn’t the way to escape it. We ought to replace the old simplification with something wiser, which would work in both the old situation and the new. But before we think to do that, we’ve often gone through other trials and layered other fakery on top of the original fakery.[^8] This makes a larger mess that is even harder to backtrack.

series-unclenching-practice::34.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::34.snippetHtml: In the short term, it’s easier to add just one more patch to deal with the newest challenge, than to untangle the whole mess and rebuild things more sensibly. And how can I even start to take an outside view of what “more sensibly” could mean, when all the ways I can experience the world are already embedded in a monstrous patchwork that no longer even registers as a mess to me?

series-unclenching-practice::35.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::35.snippetHtml:
Let’s say a person has 10 different mental constructs (beliefs) that they use to make sense of their situation and employ strategies for getting their needs met. That these beliefs strongly resist updating in light of new evidence makes perfect sense in the context in which any one of the beliefs changing makes the whole structure worse than before. The idea that there is a much better way of being somewhere far away in mind architecture space requires quite a bit of faith. Or, as weird sun twitter put it: “‘That way lies madness’ He said, pointing in all possible directions from the center of the attractor.” So the beliefs resist change by virtue of being load bearing, by having had lots of important structures built on top of them. To change them would feel like invalidating the suffering that one (or others) underwent to attain meaningful outcomes within that framework.

  • Romeo Stevens, “(mis)Translating the Buddha”

series-unclenching-practice::36.snippetHtml: Let’s say a person has 10 different mental constructs (beliefs) that they use to make sense of their situation and employ strategies for getting their needs met. series-unclenching-practice::39.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::39.snippetHtml: When I finally try to untangle my mess, and gain insight to loosen some tension or untie some knot, I also alter the tensions in the surrounding weave. Unexpected things may happen. Sometimes a load-bearing beam[^9] or a section of scaffolding collapses, and I have to put in the work to restructure, or risk a larger collapse.

series-unclenching-practice::40.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::40.snippetHtml:
Dissolving the constructs that lead to you prioritizing exercise, eating well, and sleeping should be seen as dissolution of the goodness of the means, not the ends. e.g. you were using fear based motivation to keep you exercising, which you subsequently saw through. This doesn't mean exercise was bad, it means your method was bad and you should find an upgraded one.

  • Romeo Stevens, “Why do contemplative practitioners make so many metaphysical claims?”

series-unclenching-practice::42.snippetHtml: • Romeo Stevens, “Why do contemplative practitioners make so many metaphysical claims?”

series-unclenching-practice::43.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::43.snippetHtml: Romeo Stevens, “Why do contemplative practitioners make so many metaphysical claims?”

series-unclenching-practice::44.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::44.snippetHtml: The jhānas are worth dwelling on for a moment. On the surface they seem kind of concerning. You’re saying if I just step back from all the other stuff I do with my life, I can manufacture extremely pure and potent positive vibes for myself? Yes, pretty much. Isn’t that just wireheading? No, not quite. Why not? Won’t I get addicted? Well, in principle these vibes can be abused, but according to Romeo Stevens: “every teacher who I trust reports that this is pretty rare, and much more likely to happen to people who practice without the feedback of a teacher and community”.

series-unclenching-practice::45.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::45.snippetHtml: I’ve not reached the jhānas yet, but I’m also not particularly worried about them. Why?

series-unclenching-practice::46.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::46.snippetHtml: Because of the nature of falling-in, and my tendency to treat feelings as essences of whichever familiar objects or situations “give” me the feelings, there’s a tyranny those objects[^10] can hold over my mind. The jhānas make it plain that this is an illusion. The pure feelings were in me all along! Freed from the need to pursue any particular object, I can learn about the feeling itself, unconditionally. In doing so, I’ll tend to grow further beyond the compulsive grabby quest for pleasure, and into the peace of the realization that enjoyment can be everywhere and nowhere—and that nothing can hold me hostage to it. This isn’t the usual kind of easy trick I could abuse to get a hit of feeling, only later to be left wanting.

series-unclenching-practice::47.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::47.snippetHtml: The jhānas take patience. I expect them to deepen and purify my appreciation and capacity for joy. From the vantage of the jhānas I expect to be more able to cultivate insight, clarity, and the motivation to share in the freedom I find. But I can’t share this freedom simply by dwelling in positive vibes. I have to stand up and head back into the world—there are still problems to solve, and I don’t want to ignore them for feelings of boundless rapture and tranquility.

series-unclenching-practice::48.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::48.snippetHtml: What if vulnerable or corruptible people find the jhānas? Oh… but what if we don’t find the jhānas?

series-unclenching-practice::49.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::49.snippetHtml:
Life is everywhere life, life in ourselves, not in what is outside us.

  • Dostoevsky (letter to his brother, on the day of his mock execution)

series-unclenching-practice::50.snippetHtml: Life is everywhere life, life in ourselves, not in what is outside us.

series-unclenching-practice::53.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::53.snippetHtml: How might we squeeze the different types of practice into the categories we’ve already seen in this series? This might not be absolutely correct, but maybe it will yield some insight.

series-unclenching-practice::54.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::54.snippetHtml: Concentration practice kind of looks like leaning in to certain mental states, and making them more stable or robust. Practitioners would tend to say this shouldn’t look effortful—fine, okay.

series-unclenching-practice::55.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::55.snippetHtml: Importantly, this doesn’t usually mean leaning into just any mental states, like Taylor Swift earworms, Sunday brunch FOMO, or fantasy league planning. These would all count as fallings-in. They don’t fit our purpose. We want to practice entering states that it might be useful to enter again later. But perhaps more importantly, we want practices that are meta-unclenchy.

series-unclenching-practice::56.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::56.snippetHtml: … what? Well, practicing concentration means flexing certain states, and in principle this could turn into pull-too-hard-on-the-finger-trap style clenching. But we can choose a type of narrowing that tends to lead back into a widening. This is kind of like cleaning your room[^11]: the act of cleaning itself is narrowing, and might be stressful at first, but the context it creates is freeing. Cleaning can be a bit clenchy, but it’s also meta-unclenchy.

series-unclenching-practice::57.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::57.snippetHtml: In contrast to concentration practice, insight practice is more about directly leaning out from any particular mental state that could inhibit the emergence of patterns to be observed, noted, or contemplated. Just unclench, and let things happen. Don’t contract too long or hard on any of them, but watch how they move and disturb and relate to each other. Practicing insight means fishing for the position of our thoughts in their larger context, and for those “Aha!” moments that reveal the patterns we’re trapped in. To continue with an imperfect and too-small metaphor: insight is like looking at your room, and letting your imagination run wild about how you’d rearrange the furniture[^12].

series-unclenching-practice::58.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::58.snippetHtml: Concentration helps with insight because there’s much more clarity and pleasure in reimagining and disrupting the order of things, when they aren’t covered in dirt and cobwebs. Cleaning and rearranging are synergistic.

series-unclenching-practice::59.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::59.snippetHtml: So there is a kind of duality between concentration practices and insight practices. One seeks to purify our attention, the other to unsettle it. And kind of like there’s a trade-off between exploit versus explore, and a trade-off between structure-forcing stubbornness versus structure-fitting science, there is a balance between concentration and insight.

series-unclenching-practice::60.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::60.snippetHtml: Stevens mentions that too much concentration practice can cause “stuck” feelings. Well, concentration practices exploit certain focused states, which creates room for exploration. But if we don’t eventually use that space for exploration… that’s like always cleaning your room, but never rearranging anything. Living in the same sterile space, forever.

series-unclenching-practice::61.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::61.snippetHtml: And too much insight practice can “[stir] up trauma and not [deal] with it”, which is what happens when we explore too much without creating a context in which we are happy to exploit the results of our search. This is kind of like pacing around your dirty room every week, thinking of how to rearrange it. Mostly you just eat dust and become discouraged.

series-unclenching-practice::62.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::62.snippetHtml: Should we expect things to be quite so binary? Healthy behaviour often isn’t. Still, specific meditative practices may be kind of lopsided, at least in the beginning.

series-unclenching-practice::63.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::63.snippetHtml:
Most meditation systems are depth-first: you plunge, deeply, into one area of your mind—by, say, learning how to concentrate on your breath with heroic clarity—and then you take the mental machinery thus developed and try to iron out your life with it.

  • Sasha Chapin

series-unclenching-practice::64.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::64.snippetHtml: Most meditation systems are depth-first: you plunge, deeply, into one area of your mind—by, say, learning how to concentrate on your breath with heroic clarity—and then you take the mental machinery thus developed and try to iron out your life with it.

series-unclenching-practice::67.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::67.snippetHtml: A role of integration practices is to monitor the usefulness and moderate the balance of the specific meditative practices we pick up, by keeping them in contact with the rest of our lives. Of course, different sets of practices will work better for different people with different problems at different times. We should want to choose practices that form tight feedback loops and bring noticeable improvements to our problems. If we can’t see this happening, we leave those practices behind, or try to balance them better.

series-unclenching-practice::68.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::68.snippetHtml: No surprise, but too much integration practice can also be problematic, leading to “endless analysis and working on oneself but never really getting to big shifts”. On its own, non-meditative integration doesn’t provide enough intensity or clarity to overcome our mundane inertia—it happily settles into just another activity we can fall into.

series-unclenching-practice::69.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::69.snippetHtml: We can reflectively apply our insight about property illusions and not-just-falling-in, to our meditative practices themselves[^13]: *Useful change is not a literal property of a meditative practice, but something a practice might accelerate. “*Meditation” isn’t just a button I can push to get a desirable result. My practice is built up of little behaviours—sit there, close eyes, breathe deep, observe thoughts—that I can clench on and over-emphasize just like any other behaviours, even when the immediate consequences of my practice might seem especially calming and virtuous. If I neglect to keep making this reflection—what am I really using this for, what direction am I moving, and is it staying relevant?—I might stagnate, or worse, fixate on the delightful power of a newfound accelerator until I accelerate right into a wall, or off a cliff.[^14] In less extreme terms: a practice can become a fakery like any other. There’s no guarantee it won’t worsen my mess, my technical debt. I should keep reflecting.

series-unclenching-practice::70.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::70.snippetHtml:
[Mark Lippmann’s meditation system[^15]] is breadth-first: he wants you to mindfully do a whole bunch of different little things—small intentional changes in your thinking, exploration of different states, reflection, reverie—and thus take a million little steps towards the goal of understanding the way you function.

  • Sasha Chapin

series-unclenching-practice::71.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::71.snippetHtml: [Mark Lippmann’s meditation system[^15]] is breadth-first: he wants you to mindfully do a whole bunch of different little things—small intentional changes in your thinking, exploration of different states, reflection, reverie—and thus take a million little steps towards the goal of understanding the way you function.

series-unclenching-practice::74.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::74.snippetHtml:
But meditation […] will give you some extra tools and perceptual clarity around negative patterns. It won't magically eliminate the work you have to do to tinker with those patterns and implement better patterns. It does have a tendency to make that work feel less aversive.

  • Romeo Stevens, “Orientation on the Contemplative Path”

series-unclenching-practice::75.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::75.snippetHtml: But meditation […] will give you some extra tools and perceptual clarity around negative patterns. It won't magically eliminate the work you have to do to tinker with those patterns and implement better patterns. It does have a tendency to make that work feel less aversive.

series-unclenching-practice::78.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::78.snippetHtml: The usual “social animal” advice applies: keeping up with friends is a superior source of motivation to continue with practice, and to do it well. The most important antidote to meditation risks may be participation in a community of teachers, “noble friends”, and therapists. It’s not difficult to set a trap for yourself that’s all-but-invisible to you alone. A small conversation with an honest and perceptive person can be a powerful seed for insights. Let’s cover each other’s blind spots.

series-unclenching-practice::79.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::79.snippetHtml: Not all community is equal. There’s danger in applying powerful accelerants of self-alteration when the feedback you get is overconfident (everything will be better if you do X, it worked for me!) or isn’t really feedback at all (you do you!!). It’s important that the friends and communities you relate to in your practice should value pragmatism and skepticism at least as much as metaphysics and spirituality.

series-unclenching-practice::80.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::80.snippetHtml:
In my personal opinion, shooting openness sky high without a balancing increase in healthy skepticism reliably lands you in whacky belief town. Most practitioners are not starting with solid prerequisites about map-territory distinctions, probabilistic over binary reasoning, and strong ability to demarcate is and ought (positive and normative) claims. Most schools are not, in my experience, emphasizing the very skeptical nature of the Buddha's inquiry into his own mental processing.

  • Romeo Stevens, “Why do contemplative practitioners make so many metaphysical claims?”

series-unclenching-practice::82.snippetHtml: • Romeo Stevens, “Why do contemplative practitioners make so many metaphysical claims?”

series-unclenching-practice::83.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::83.snippetHtml: Romeo Stevens, “Why do contemplative practitioners make so many metaphysical claims?”

series-unclenching-practice::84.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::84.snippetHtml: It’s easy to forget that our feelings are intrinsic to us, and not the things and people that are most familiar to us. So we keep falling into our lives, and into a kind of private tyranny.

series-unclenching-practice::85.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::85.snippetHtml: Confronted with urgent or difficult problems, we find good-enough solutions even if they are patches atop patches. This makes a mess of our minds, until the mess becomes familiar and forgotten.

series-unclenching-practice::86.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::86.snippetHtml: Meditation is about spending some time not doing these things—mentally “cleaning your room”, and finding a clarity in which it’s a pleasure to witness how things are arranged, and then to imagine rearranging them for the better.

series-unclenching-practice::87.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::87.snippetHtml: We might consider three categories of practice: concentration, insight, and integration. Too much of any one of them could be problematic.

series-unclenching-practice::88.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::88.snippetHtml: We want to actually solve problems. Sometimes, meditative practices can accelerate that. But what are we accelerating towards? It’s crucial to continually, reflectively judge our choice and balance of practices, and the direction we are heading. Being part of a community of skeptical practitioners is invaluable for covering blind spots and keeping up motivation.

series-unclenching-practice::89.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::89.snippetHtml: I haven’t described how to engage in specific practices in this post, which is only a survey of ideas. I’m no expert, and you can find much more detail elsewhere, e.g. from Shinzen Young.

series-unclenching-practice::90.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::90.snippetHtml: In the next part: the language of Buddhism.

series-unclenching-practice::92.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::92.snippetHtml: [^1]: Who am I to say anyone is trapped? How do I know what they’re going through, or what they want?

series-unclenching-practice::93.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::93.snippetHtml: Well, why do I think a child caught in a finger trap might eventually want to escape? Except the child is now an adult, and perhaps offended or embarrassed to consider they might still be ensnared. They might even have some inspiring stories about the virtues of living in prison.

series-unclenching-practice::94.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::94.snippetHtml: In this case, I choose to be stubborn: trauma and spite can complicate people in ways they never would have chosen freely. Is our submission to these complications an equally valid aspect of freedom? In fact the desire for freedom is a rebellion against them. But of course, it doesn’t help to try to coerce people to stop rationalizing themselves back into their predicaments. I can’t force people to be free, but I can gesture at the absurdity.

series-unclenching-practice::95.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::95.snippetHtml: Some traps we can simply be helped out of. Others are up to us to notice, in ourselves. Good words are one way to begin.

series-unclenching-practice::96.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::96.snippetHtml: [^2]: What about depression, self-loathing, “I hate my job”, etc.? The situation is not so different, except in the specific patterns of inertia—a kind of inertia-killing inertia. Rather than excitement, the “expectation for the next episode” is some more dismal prediction.

series-unclenching-practice::97.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::97.snippetHtml: [^3]: Perhaps you’re fortunate that your life has settled into harmony without this happening much, and everything you keep falling-into is just fine with you. If so, I’d merely ask how you know how you’d react, if all of that fell apart? And how do you know it won’t?

series-unclenching-practice::98.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::98.snippetHtml: [^4]: This is kind of analogous to certain techniques of clinical psychology, like cognitive behavioural therapy—which begin with witnessing how feelings and actions lead into each other.

series-unclenching-practice::99.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::99.snippetHtml: [^5]: To let go, in a sense. But what if letting go means I lose? Well, it doesn’t generally mean that, or you never would have learned how to win in the first place. You’d never have pushed inward on that finger trap, and found out how to escape.

series-unclenching-practice::100.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::100.snippetHtml: It does feel scary to stop pulling on something you’ve always pulled on. Am I making a mistake? Pulling has always worked for me. Well, it is possible you’ll make a mistake. Changing yourself isn’t risk-free. More on that in a moment.

series-unclenching-practice::101.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::101.snippetHtml: [^6]: I recognize the irony in using stories to explain practices that might help us to escape from stories—and to use language to talk about the limits of language. This is inevitable and it’s OK, as long as we don’t grasp at any particular story for too long.

series-unclenching-practice::102.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::102.snippetHtml: [^7]: See Sasha Chapin and Autodereify for a reviews of Lippmann’s book-length website.

series-unclenching-practice::103.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::103.snippetHtml: [^8]: Weirdly, this is kind of like how evolution accumulates changes in our biology—it tends to move forward, elaborating incrementally on what is already there, and not making sweeping erasures.

series-unclenching-practice::104.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::104.snippetHtml: [^9]: I ought to be careful with these metaphors. The mind is often shaped in many more dimensions than textiles or buildings are.

series-unclenching-practice::105.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::105.snippetHtml: [^10]: In this case “object” includes people—we’re discussing a phenomenon of objectification.

series-unclenching-practice::106.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::106.snippetHtml: It also includes rewarding substances such as alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, and opioids.

series-unclenching-practice::107.title: Practice (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-practice::107.snippetHtml: [^11]: This metaphor is kind of layered, since cleaning your literal room can help set up the unburdened sensory states that are useful for meditation; and if you do not practice entering concentrated meditative states (and especially if you are depressed) it can be harder to notice or care that your literal room is dirty.

series-unclenching-practice::108.title: Practice (Unclenching)

Of course, it is generally good to take the reflective skepticism about practices as far as you can, without wrecking your ability to problem-solve.

series-unclenching-unclenching::1.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::1.snippetHtml: It’s playtime. I reach for my favourite toy, but something unexpected messes with me. Some other kid's hand suddenly appears from the side and nudges mine, fudging my movement. I adapt and continue: I really want my toy. Maybe I get it. Sometimes the other kid does.

series-unclenching-unclenching::2.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::2.snippetHtml: Similar incidents repeat several times over a few days of preschool. Meanwhile, an adult watches from across the room. She notices that whenever the other kid is around, I tense up a bit, my movements a little more jerky, furtive.

series-unclenching-unclenching::4.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::4.snippetHtml: Have you ever played with one of these? Then you'd know their trick: once you put your fingers in, you can't simply pull them out. But that's probably what you'd try, your first time playing with one. It makes sense. Pulling is effective for many cases of trapped fingers, including all the usual ones you'd seen before. You pull, and the trap tightens as it lengthens. It grips your fingers harder, and they won't come out! Ugh.

series-unclenching-unclenching::5.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::5.snippetHtml: Now here's the interesting part: just like you have an action (pull) ready to exploit when your fingers are trapped, you also have a "meta-action" ready when you encounter frustration: try harder.

series-unclenching-unclenching::7.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::7.snippetHtml: Of course, you eventually learn that the only clean way out is to relax. To fall apart. To see and act anew.

series-unclenching-unclenching::8.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)

series-unclenching-unclenching::9.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::9.snippetHtml: One recent summer afternoon, I visited some friends, parents of a 4-year-old daughter. We were eating and talking on the deck behind their house with a few others. At first, mom and daughter were away.

series-unclenching-unclenching::10.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::10.snippetHtml: After a couple of hours, they returned. But daughter was scared to come into the backyard and up onto the deck. Mom, who is one of the most understanding and gentle people I've met, carries daughter up onto the deck and sits with her for a while. The entire time, she's burying her face and half-crying, begging to be carried inside. Mom says she's free to go in, but she won't be carried. Mom reminds her that the rest of us are harmless. She doesn't seem to believe it.

series-unclenching-unclenching::11.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::11.snippetHtml: Eventually she gets tired and goes in. For a time, she sneaks glances at us from the window. Before long, she comes back out and plays on the trampoline with her older brother, apparently unworried.

series-unclenching-unclenching::12.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::12.snippetHtml: At some point, she forgot to hold onto her fear.

series-unclenching-unclenching::13.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::13.snippetHtml: Near the beginning of the pandemic, I consumed a neuroscience paper I couldn’t quite digest. Before long, I was ruminating[^1] on philosophy.

series-unclenching-unclenching::14.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::14.snippetHtml: On the surface, the paper asked how we can move our limbs effectively when under the influence of unpredictable forces. But the results nudged me toward a deeper principle, one I'd noticed in myself and suspected in everyone, obvious in the movements of our bodies but also those of our minds.

series-unclenching-unclenching::15.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-unclenching::15.snippetHtml: For a time, the principle was nameless and unspoken. Then, after chewing for a while on visions of muscles, I settled on a metaphor: clenching.

series-unclenching-unclenching::21.snippetHtml: How clenchy! How utterly locked in. How alone, leaning into a strategy that’d never have me try something fresh outside.

series-unclenching-unclenching::22.title: Unclenching (Unclenching)

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: This post is part of a series.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: During a recent conversation about how best to situate my use of the word "clenching" to respect existing knowledge and terms, Cube Flipper mentioned an uncanny parallel with the Buddhist concept of taṇhā, and suggested I read Romeo Stevens’ post (mis)Translating the Buddha.[^1] It was my first encounter with his writing, and the first time I really engaged with any writing about meditative practice.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Stevens explains how the conventional Western translations of Buddhist psychological terms are largely ill-chosen, even harmfully so.[^2] He gives revised definitions for some terms from the Pali canon, a major text of Early Buddhism. He emphasizes that these terms refer to identifiable mental events, not to vague metaphysical energies, like we might mistake "impermanence".

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Tanha is the cause of Dukkha. Understanding Anicca and Anatta inclines the mind toward Nibbana by removing the Upadana that maintains the creation of Sankharas.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Tanha is the cause of Dukkha. Understanding Anicca and Anatta inclines the mind toward Nibbana by removing the Upadana that maintains the creation of Sankharas.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: The above sentence full of Pali terms is about detectable mental events within the stream of physical sensation, feeling tones, mental talk, and mental image that makes up moment to moment experience. If something sounds weird it's just that you've never reified it before because it goes by very fast (10-40hz range). Meditation is about training the mind to be able to notice these more subtle events and then instructions for noticing certain things about the causal relationship between these subtle events and how good your moment to moment experience really is. The purpose of meditation is not to become a really good meditator, to experience certain cool temporary states (though some are helpful), etc. But direct insight into the basic building blocks of your experience.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: I recommend reading through the entire post. Let’s walk through some parts of it and relate them to what we’ve already seen in this series: clenching, or robustening, or predicting too hard.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Before we begin, we’d better start by considering whether different people will even experience the same basic classes of mental events. Are some shared universally, and already waiting to be noted in the workings of each of our minds? Or are they created like self-fulfilling prophecies, as patterns that meditators incept in themselves under the influence of culture and memes? How consistent is human phenomenology?

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: I haven't had much time yet to digest the terms we’ll discuss. How might they refer to things I've already noticed about the movements of my mind? Do some of them refer to things I've never noticed? Maybe. I guess I'll have to meditate more. Will I notice which new things I create that weren’t there before?

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: I’m not sure. For now, I remain confused. I’m writing this to air out my current understanding and confusion.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Which brings us to one more preliminary moment of skepticism. Remember that we tend to take on technical debt? We’re evolved animals, impulsive about pushing through, enduring immediate encounters by any means, more than slowing down to perfect our minds before we act. We pile on OK solutions that work well enough for now. The more we’re stressed or uncertain, the harder we lean into the mess of good-enoughs we already have, patching and patching them instead of feeling free to stop to untangle and consolidate them.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Well, we’re also that way with words and ideas. So we should be wary of using semi-formal language to talk about the kinds of mental events that precede language. It is easy enough for a mind to objectify something it fancies about itself… to reify, to substitute something real with merely your idea of it. When we give our ideas names and build them into stories, they can achieve their own stable lives in our attention, even if the things they were originally intended to reference aren’t so stable themselves, or even real.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Sometimes we lean in a little too much, stubbornly steamrolling the subtlety of reality beneath our too-solid story of it.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml:
A lot of the confusing stuff in buddhism is trying to talk about these direct insights. e.g. 'grasping' isn't talking about a cognitive understanding but rather a direct perception of an automatic mental move that happens in the pre-conscious perceptual stack (at least pre-conscious prior to a bunch of work). Buddhists do this because sometimes, if a person is ready, you can speed things up by just pointing the thing out rather than waiting for them to figure it out all on their own. […]

I do think that this has resulted in ambient memetic immunity of the same type hypothesized by Scott Alexander and others about why new psychotherapy methods work for a while and then seem to stop working. People get some sort of idea of what all these experiences are supposed to be and as a result ignore actual moment to moment sensation.

  • Romeo Stevens, “Dukkha: created vs discovered”

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Romeo Stevens, “Dukkha: created vs discovered”

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Sometimes you can make prophecies come true by faking it. But if you really want insight into the workings of your mind, you can’t keep dressing them up in stories. Your actual mental events are not your firstborn concepts of those events, nor your second-born, nor hundredth.[^3] Eventually my perceptions and ideas and words may reach a sufficient approximation of nuance that their interplay can do good work to relate some of my inner movements. But that’s secondary to learning to pay any attention to those movements, as long as I’m concerned with actual introspective competence. If you lean too hard or too often on any particular story about what an experience should be, perhaps you’ve acquired a piece of identity that may stubbornly override your capacity for honest experiences.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: So each time you discover a pleasantly novel personal insight or meditative state, if you find yourself excited to name it and hold it and keep it: beware the little debt trap you might be building.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.title: Who (mis)translates the (mis)translators? (Unclenching)
series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml:
The investigation you do into your own experience has to be a real investigation, and not one in which you are highly confident about what there is to find. i.e. people feel like they're meditating wrong if their experience doesn't seem to match whichever map they are using.

  • Romeo Stevens, “Dukkha: created vs discovered”

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Of course that doesn’t mean you can or should abandon words and ideas completely. Just, maybe don’t grasp them so quickly or hold them so tightly.

series-unclenching-who-mistranslates-the.snippetHtml: Don’t flee so fast from confusion.
